(p-2) Surat al-Ra'd is Medinan, though it is said to be Meccan except for His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾ to the end of the verse. Its verses number forty-three.

﴿Al-Mr﴾ is a name for the surah. Its position (i'rab) may be either nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this surah is named by this name. This is more evident than taking it as nominative by way of being a subject, since the proper name has not been preceded by the naming, as has been mentioned many times. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Tilka﴾ ("those") according to the first reading is an independent subject. According to the second reading, it is a second subject, or an apposition to the first, pointed to by it to indicate its grandeur. Or its position may be accusative, by supposing a verb that suits the context, such as "recite" or "remember," so that ﴿tilka﴾ is a subject, just as when "al-Mr" is recited in the manner of enumeration. Or it means: God knows best. "And I see" (wa-ara), according to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, and the predicate in all these suppositions is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the verses of the Book﴾, that is, of the wondrous, perfect Book, which needs no description by attribute, which is known as such among the books, and which deserves that the name "Book" be restricted to it. Thus it is an expression for the whole Qur'an, or for the whole that was revealed at that time, as has been mentioned at the beginning of Surat Yunus, since this is what is understood from the unqualified term "Book" that needs no qualifier. By this it becomes clear what is meant by describing the verses with the attributes of perfection that are ascribed to what they are attached to. This is unlike the case where it is made an expression for the surah, for the surah does not enjoy such fame in being described by that, which would make an explicit description unnecessary. Moreover, it would be an expression for all its verses, so it would be necessary to make "tilka" a pointer to each one of them individually, and in this there is what is not hidden of the forced interpretation whose details were mentioned in Surat Yunus. ﴿And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, that is, the aforementioned Book in its entirety, not this surah alone.

﴿The truth﴾: the established, which corresponds to reality in everything it states, and which deserves to have truthfulness specially attributed to it because of its preeminence in it. There is nothing in it indicating that what is other than it is not true at all. Furthermore, its truthfulness entails the truthfulness of all the other heavenly scriptures, since it confirms what is before it and watches over it. In the expression of it by the relative pronoun, and the ascription of the sending down to it in the passive form, and the mention of the attribute of lordship as an annex to his pronoun, peace be upon him, there is an indication of the grandeur of what was sent down, following from the majesty of the status of the One who sent it down, and the honoring of the one to whom it was sent, and an allusion to the reason for building the predicate, which is not hidden.

﴿But most people do not believe﴾ in that manifest truth, due to their neglect of looking into it and reflecting upon it. Thus their non-belief relates to the aspect of its truthfulness, since that is the basis for affirmation and denial, not to the aspect of its being sent down, as has been said. And because it comes in the manner of description rather than information.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 2:

﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens﴾ (p-3) That is: He created them elevated, in the manner of their saying: "Glory be to Him who made the elephant great and the gnat small." It does not mean that He raised them after they had not been so. The clause is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar), like His saying: "And He it is who spread out the earth" ﴿without pillars﴾, that is: without supports. It is the plural of 'imad (pillar), like ihab and ahab, and it is that by which something is propped up, i.e., supported. It is said: "I propped up the wall" (amadtu al-ha'it), meaning: I buttressed it. It has also been read ('umud), as the plural of 'amud, with the meaning of 'imad, like rusul and rasul. The use of the plural form for the heavens is not because the negation applies to each of them as a pillar and not as a support.

﴿You see them﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), cited as evidence for what was mentioned about the raising of the heavens without pillars. It has been said that it is an attribute of "pillars" (amad), introduced to create an impression of uncertainty, because they have pillars that are not visible, namely the power of Allah the Exalted. ﴿Then He istawa﴾, that is: He took control (istawla) ﴿over the Throne﴾ by preserving and governing, or His command istawa. Our companions (Ash'aris) hold that istiwa' over the Throne is an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, without modality (bila kayf). Whatever the case, the intended meaning is not an intention to bring the Throne into existence or create it, so there is no need to take the particle "thumma" (then) to indicate a delay in rank.

﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾: He made them submissive, and made them obedient to what is intended for them of motions and other things.

﴿Each﴾ of the sun and the moon ﴿runs﴾ as intended for them ﴿for a specified term﴾, for a determined period, in which their cycle is completed, like the year for the sun and the month for the moon; for each of them runs every day on a specific one of the daily orbits, or for a period at the end of which their motions cease and all that is intended from them passes from potential to actuality, or for a goal at which this is completed. The clause explains the wisdoms behind their subjection.

﴿He regulates﴾ the affair with what He has made of raising, istiwa' and subjection, that is: He decrees and determines according to what wisdom and benefit require. ﴿The affair﴾, the affair of all creation and the affair of His dominion and lordship. ﴿He details the signs﴾, the indications of the perfection of His power and the far-reaching of His wisdom, that is: He brings them forth in detail, and they are the wondrous acts mentioned, and the celestial configurations that follow them, arising gradually, which entail strange effects in the sublunary realm according to the requirement of the governing and determining. Thus the two clauses may be: either circumstantial clauses (hal) relating to the pronoun in istawa, with His saying "And He subjected the sun and the moon" being a continuation of the istiwa'; or they may be explanatory of it. Or the first is a circumstantial clause from it, and the second from the pronoun within it; or both are from the pronouns of the mentioned verbs.

His saying "Each runs for a specified term" is either a continuation of the subjection, or two predicates regarding His saying "Allah" as one predicate after another, with the relative clause serving as an attribute of the subject; it is brought in to indicate the affirmation of the predicate and the magnification of its importance, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

؎ Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mightier and loftier.

﴿So that you﴾ upon witnessing them and discovering their details, ﴿with the meeting of your Lord﴾, with encountering Him for recompense, ﴿may be certain﴾. For whoever contemplates them with true contemplation becomes certain that He who is able to originate these wondrous crafts is capable of all things, and that these firm arrangements have consequences and ends that must be reached. It has been made clear through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, that this is the testing of the responsible, then their recompense according to their deeds; therefore there is necessarily certainty regarding the recompense. And when he had established the heavenly evidences, he followed them with mention of the terrestrial proofs, saying:

He it is who spread out the earth: [i.e., He] extended it lengthwise and widthwise. Al-Asamm said: *al-madd* (spreading out) is extending something to a point whose end cannot be reached, and so it indicates the vastness of its expanse and the breadth of its regions.

﴿And He placed in it firm mountains﴾: i.e., mountains fixed in their places, stable (*rusuww*, settling), which is the steadiness of heavy bodies. The noun being described (*al-mawsuf*, the qualified noun) is not mentioned, because the predominance of its use as an adjective (*ghalabat al-wasf*) makes it unnecessary. The restriction of the plural of *fa'il* to the form *fawa'il* to *fawaris* (horsemen), *hawalik* (perishers), and *nawakis* (those who bow their heads) applies only to the attributes of rational beings. For other things, this pattern is not observed at all, as in God's words: ﴿days numbered﴾ and His words: ﴿The pilgrimage is in known months﴾, and so on. Therefore there is no need to make its singular form an adjective of the paucity plural (*jam' al-qilla*), namely *ajbul*. Rather, it is considered a plural of abundance (*jam' al-kathra*), namely *jibal*, whose arrangement includes a group of paucity plurals, with each of them treated as its singular. As has been said, however, there is no room for this, since the plurality of each of the two plural forms is only considered with respect to the individuals under it, not with respect to the paucity plural's arrangement of individuals or the abundance plural's arrangement of paucity plurals. Each of them is the plural of *jabal* (mountain); *jibal* is not the plural of *ajbul*, just as *ta'ifa* plurals are *ta'ifa*. Nor is there any need to resort to counting the aforementioned adjective, by predominance, among the nouns that are pluralized as *fawa'il*, as one opinion holds, since that is baseless, because predominance applies only to the plural and not to the singular. The expression of the mountains by this title is to show that the settling of the earth's stability branches from their firmness.

﴿and rivers﴾: wide channels. What is meant is the water flowing in them. Their being governed together with the mountains by a single verb indicates that the mountains are the source of the rivers, and it explains another benefit of the mountains besides their function of keeping the earth from the agitation that would disrupt the stability of footing and the movement of animals. This benefit branches from the animals' settling and moving, namely their livelihood through water and pasture.

﴿And of all the fruits﴾: this is connected to *ja'ala* (He placed) in His words ﴿He placed in it two mates, two﴾, i.e., two in a true sense of duality. They are two individuals, each of which is the mate of the other. The phrase *zawjayn ithnayn* (two mates, two) is emphasized so that it is not understood that the intended meaning is the even numbers (*ash-shaf'an*), since *zawj* is used for a set. However, this duality is a notional (*i'tibariyya*) duality: He made from every kind of fruit present in the world two types, two classes, either in color, like white and black; or in taste, like sweet and sour; or in size, like small and large; or in quality, like hot and cold, and similar things. It is permissible for this phrase to be connected to the first *ja'ala*, and for the second to be a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) explaining the manner of that making.

﴿He covers the night over the day﴾: this is a relational metaphor (*isti'ara tab'iyya tamthiliyya*), based on comparing the removal of the light of the atmosphere to darkness, by covering visible things with coverings. That is, He veils the day with night, and the construction (*al-tarkib*). Although the reverse is also possible, by taking the second object as preceding the first, since the light of day also conceals the darkness of night, the more appropriate reading for night is that it is the one that covers. This is counted among the lower signs (*al-ayat al-suflIyya*), although its connection to the upper signs (*al-ayat al-ulwiyya*) is evident, in view of the fact that its appearance is on the earth, since night is only the earth's shadow, and above the point of its shadow there is no night at all. Also, night and day have a relation to the fruits in terms of their ripening and maturing, and they are also two opposite mates, like them. It is read (*yughashshi*) with a doubled *shin*, from *taghshiya* (covering).

﴿Indeed in that﴾: i.e., in what has been mentioned of the spreading of the earth and its stabilization with the firm mountains, the flowing of the rivers, the creation of the fruits, and the covering of night over day. The use of the demonstrative *dhalika* (that) indicates the great importance of what is pointed to in its domain. ﴿are signs﴾ dazzling, i.e., they are the effects of those wondrous acts, the wisdom of their Maker being exalted. So *fi* (in) retains its literal meaning, since those effects are settled in those acts and depend on them. It is also permissible that *dhalika* refers to those effects that are implied by those acts, and then *fi* is abstractive (*tajridiyya*).

﴿for a people who reflect﴾: for reflecting upon them leads to the judgment that the formation of each of these, in this elegant pattern and fitting method, necessarily requires a capable, wise creator who does what He wills and chooses what He desires, and whose judgment none can reverse. He is the Praiseworthy, the Glorious.

(p-5) ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts﴾: this is a resumed sentence (jumla musta'nafa) comprising another group of signs, i.e., many plots of land differing in their qualities: from good to salt-laden (sabkha), from fertile (karima) to poor (zahida), from hard (sulba) to soft (rikhwa), and other than that.

﴿Neighbouring (mutajawirat)﴾ means adjoining one another. In some copies of the Qur'an the word is read as "mutajawiratin" (in the accusative), meaning: He placed in the earth tracts (qit'an) that are neighbouring.

﴿And gardens of vines﴾ means many orchards among them; ﴿and tillage﴾ of every kind of grain. Its being singular (zar') takes into account its origin (asl). Perhaps the mention of the gardens before it, although it is the pillar of livelihood, is due to the clear evidence of their condition in their diversity, their distinction from the rest, and the firmness of this in them; and the delaying of His words, exalted is He, ﴿and palm trees﴾, is so that there does not fall between them and their attribute, which is His words, exalted is He, ﴿Some are multiple-stemmed and some single-stemmed﴾, anything intervening. The word sinwan (sinwān) is the plural of sinw, like qinwan and qinw, and it refers to a palm tree that has two heads while its root is one. It is also read with a ḍamma on the ṣād according to the dialect of the Banu Tamim and Qays. It is also read "jannat" (gardens) in the accusative, coordinated with "zawjayn" (two kinds), and in the genitive, governed by "kull al-thamarat" (of all the fruits). Perhaps the non-arrangement of His words, exalted is He, ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts﴾, in this thread, although the particularity of each of those tracts with its conditions and attributes is by the sheer making of the Wise Creator, exalted is His power, when He spread the earth and smoothed it out, is an allusion to the fact that those conditions are firmly established attributes of those tracts. It is also read "wa-zar'in wa-nakhilin" (and tillage and palm trees) in the genitive, coordinated with "a'nab" (vines) or "jannat" (gardens).

﴿It is watered﴾ means: what has been mentioned of the tracts, the gardens, the tillage and the palm trees. It is also read in the feminine, in consideration of the wording. The first is more fitting to the context of showing the unity of all of them in the state of irrigation, ﴿with one water﴾, there being no difference in its nature, whether the irrigation is by rainwater or by river water.

﴿And We favour﴾, along with the interlocking of the causes of similarity, by the sheer power and choice of Ourselves, ﴿some of them over others﴾ among them ﴿in fruit﴾, in what is produced from them of fruit and taste. It is also read with the letter yā' (yufaddilu), in the active voice referring back to "yudabbiru", "yufassilu" and "yughshi", and in the passive voice. In this there is what is not hidden of grandeur, and an indication that the impossibility of the act being ascribed to another agent makes the active construction unnecessary.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, which has been detailed of the states of the tracts and gardens, ﴿are signs﴾, many, great and manifest, ﴿for a people who use reason﴾, who know according to the dictates of their intellects. For whoever understands these wondrous states does not hesitate in affirming that He who is able to originate these marvels, and created those fruits differing in shapes, colours, tastes and scents, in those distinct yet adjoining tracts, and made them gardens full of delight, is able to restore what He originated. Rather, that is easier by analogy. Although these states are themselves the signs and not merely in them, their like has been abstracted from them, in exaggeration of their being a sign, so that "fī" is "tajridiyya" like its occurrence in His words, "For them therein is the abode of eternity." Or what is indicated is the universal states, and the signs are their individual instances occurring gradually over time, and their particular occurrences in regions and places observed by their people. Thus "fī" retains its meaning. And since the indication of these states toward what they signify is clearer than what preceded, the fact that they are signs is attached purely to intellection; for this reason it does not address anything beyond the favouring of some over others in the fruit, which is apparent to every reasonable person, while the realization of that in the properties and qualities, whose discovery depends on some kind of reflection and contemplation, is not mentioned, as if there were no need for reflection in that either. And there is in this an implicit rebuke that the polytheists are not reasonable.

(p-6) ﴿And if you wonder﴾, O Muhammad, at something, ﴿then wondrous﴾ (I do not wonder at it; it is truly worthy that wonder be restricted to it) ﴿is their saying﴾, after witnessing what has been enumerated for you of the signs that testify that He, exalted is He, is over all things capable.

﴿"When we are dust..."﴾ is in the form of an interrogative of denial (al-istifham al-inkari), which conveys complete remoteness and disapproval. It occupies a nominative position as an apposition (badaliyyah) to "qawluhum" (their saying), on the basis that it carries the sense of the thing said (al-maqul), or it occupies an accusative position as an object (mafu'iyyah) of it, on the basis that it is a verbal noun (masdar). So the wondrous thing, on the first reading, is their speech; on the second, it is "you wonder at them for it." The governing element (al-'amil) in "idha" (when) is what is indicated by His saying ﴿"Shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾, namely "we will be raised" or "we will be returned." The fronting of the adverbial phrase serves to strengthen the denial of resurrection by directing it to the state that contradicts it. The repetition of the hamza in their saying "a-'innā" serves to emphasize the denial. The basis of their denial is not that they would actually be established in the new creation while they are dust, but rather that they are liable to it and prepared for it. In this there is an indication of their obstinacy and persistence in rejection that is not hidden.

It has been said: "If you wonder at their saying in denying resurrection, then wondrous is their saying, and what it implies." And: "If you wonder, then you have wondered in a place of wonder." It has also been said: "And if you wonder at their denial of resurrection, then wondrous is their saying, which indicates it, so reflect." It has been permitted that the address is to everyone who is fit for it, meaning: "If you wonder, O one who looks into these signs, at the power of One whose acts are these, then increase in wonder at one who denies, despite these proofs, His power over resurrection, which is easier than these." The more fitting reading with His saying ﴿"And they ask you to hasten the evil"﴾ is the first.

His, exalted is He, saying ﴿"wondrous"﴾ is a predicate (khabar) placed before the subject (mubtada') for restriction (al-qasr) and for recording the matter from the outset, that their saying is a strange affair. It is also permissible that it be a subject (mubtada'), because it is described by the implied description, as has been pointed out. The meaning is: "And if you wonder, then the wonder is that beyond which there is no wonder." Their saying: "This is strange, so wonder at it." On the first reading: "And if you wonder, then their saying: 'This is a wonder, beyond which there is no wonder.'"

﴿Those﴾ is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the relative clause (al-mawsul) that follows, meaning: those who deny His power over resurrection, after they witnessed the manifest signs that were detailed, which compel them to faith, if they were seeing. ﴿Those who disbelieved in their Lord﴾, and persisted in that; for their denial of His power, mighty and majestic is He, is disbelief in Him, and what a disbelief it is.

﴿And those﴾ is a subject whose predicate is His saying ﴿"the shackles are on their necks"﴾, meaning: they are bound by the fetters of misguidance, whose release is not hoped for; or they will be shackled on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And those﴾, described by what has been mentioned of the attributes, ﴿are the companions of the Fire; they are therein abiding﴾, not separated from it. The placing of the separative pronoun (damir al-fasl) in the middle is not to restrict abiding forever to the deniers of resurrection alone, but to all those indicated by His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿"Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord"﴾.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 6:**

﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾: that is, the punishment with which they were warned. This was when they asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to bring the punishment upon them, mocking his warning. ﴿Before the good﴾: that is, well-being, and God's kindness to them by granting them respite.

﴿And exemplary punishments (al-mathulat) have already passed before them﴾: that is, the punishments of those like them among the deniers, so why do they not take heed from them, and guard against the same befalling them? (p-7) The circumstantial clause serves to show the feebleness of their opinion in seeking haste, mockingly. That is: they ask you to hasten it, mocking your warning and denying that what you warned them of would occur. Yet the situation is that the punishments that descended upon those like them, the deniers and the mockers, have already passed. Al-mathulah, on the pattern of al-sumrah, means a punishment; it was so named because of the resemblance (mumathalah) between it and the one punished for, and from it comes al-mithal, meaning retribution. It was read as (al-muthulat) with two damma, making the fa' follow the 'ayn. It was also read as (al-mathlat) with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the tha', as one says al-sumrah. And (al-muthlat) with a damma on the mim and a sukun on the tha', a lightened form of al-muthulat, is the plural of muthlah, like rukbah and rukbat.

﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness﴾ great ﴿for the people despite their wrongdoing﴾ against their own selves through sins and disobedience. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning: while they are wrongdoers, and the governing element in it is forgiveness. The meaning: indeed your Lord is All-Forgiving toward people; He does not hasten punishment for them even if they are wrongdoers, but gives them respite by delaying it.

﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾; He punishes whom He wills of them, when He wills. Therefore the delay of what they asked to hasten is not neglect. And it is narrated from him, peace be upon him: "Were it not for God's pardon and His overlooking, no one would have enjoyed life; and were it not for His threat and His punishment, every person would have relied (on his own deeds)."

[Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 7:]

﴿And those who disbelieve say⦆ They are also the ones who were hastening (the punishment). He shifted from the pronoun (al-idmar) to the relative form (al-mawsul) to censure them and to denounce their disbelief in the signs of God Most High, signs before which the solid mountains would crumble, since they did not give them any attention and did not regard them as belonging to the category of signs. They said: ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?⦆ like the signs of Musa and Isa, peace be upon them both, out of obstinacy and arrogance. Yet the least of the "signs that were sent down" to him, peace and blessings be upon him, is sufficient and a lesson for people of understanding (ulu al-albab).

﴿You are only a warner⦆ sent for the purpose of warning against the evil consequence of what they do and leave undone, as was the case with the messengers before you. It is not incumbent upon you except to bring that by which your prophethood is known, and this has been accomplished in a manner beyond which nothing more is needed. There is no need to oblige them or to silence them by bringing the signs they propose. ﴿And for every people there is a guide⦆ a specific one, not identified by his essence but by the title of guidance. That is: for every people there is a particular prophet who has a particular guidance, which requires the specific particularity of each of them with what is peculiar to him, for reasons known only to God; or, ﴿for every people there is a guide⦆ of great stature, capable of this, who is God, glorified is He. Your duty is only to warn them, so let not their obstinacy and their denial of the signs revealed to you concern you, nor their contempt for them. Then he followed this with what indicates the perfection of His knowledge, His power, and the comprehensiveness of His decree and destiny, both founded upon wisdom and benefit, as a reminder that the assignment of each people to a prophet, and of each prophet to a specific kind of signs, is only for the wisdoms that call for it, to manifest the perfection of His power to guide them. However, He guides only the one whose guidance is connected to His will, which follows a wisdom that He has kept to Himself. So He said: [...]

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 8:

﴿Allah knows what every female carries.﴾ That is, what she carries. Here "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and what is meant by it is what is in her womb from the time of conception (ʿulūq) until the time of birth, not only after the completion of its creation. The verb "knows" (al-ʿilm) takes one object, or "what she carries" is the object, and in whatever state it is, from among the states that come upon it one after another. In that case "ma" is an interrogative (istifhamiyyah) suspending the verb "knows," or, if it refers to the carrying itself, it is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning the act of carrying.

﴿And what the wombs diminish and what they increase.﴾ That is, what the wombs lose and what they add, in bulk and in duration. In bulk: such as the khadīj (a premature or underdeveloped birth) and the full-term child. In duration: such as the child born at the shortest period of pregnancy, the child born at the longest, and what lies between them. It is said that al-Ḍaḥḥāk was born after two years, and Haram ibn Ḥayyān after four, and for this reason he was named Haram. In number: such as one child, or more than one. It is related that Sharīk was the fourth of four (children born at once). Or what is meant is that their diminishing and increasing is known by what is in them, so the two verbs are transitive, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the water was made to subside﴾ (11:44), and His saying: ﴿And they added nine﴾ (18:25), and the saying: "it increases a camel's load (kayl baʿīr)." Or, the verbs are intransitive, and the subject is attributed to the wombs metaphorically, while the actual meaning is what is in them.

﴿And everything with Him is by measure.﴾ Among things, everything has with Him a measure (biqdar), a determined limit it cannot exceed, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created everything by measure﴾ (54:49). Every occurrence, whether substance or accident, has at every stage of the stages of creation, and at its beginnings, a specific time and a particular condition, which it scarcely exceeds. By "with Him" (ʿindiyyah) is meant the presence of knowledge, or rather presential knowledge (al-ʿilm al-ḥuḍūrī), for the realization of things in themselves, at whatever stage, whether among the stages of existence or of readiness (istiʿdād), is for Him, exalted and majestic is He, a knowledge in relation to Allah.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 13, verse 9:**

﴿Knower of the unseen﴾, i.e., that which is absent from the senses.

﴿And the witnessed﴾, i.e., that which is present to them. He expressed the two by these two terms for emphasis (mubalaghah). It has been said that by "the unseen" is meant the non-existent (المَعْدُومُ, al-ma'dum), and by "the witnessed" the existent (المَوْجُودُ, al-mawjud). This phrase is the predicate (خَبَرٌ, khabar) of an omitted subject (مُبْتَدَإٌ, mubtada'), or a predicate following another predicate. It was also read in the accusative (بِالنَّصْبِ, bi-al-nasb) as an expression of praise (عَلى المَدْحِ, 'ala al-madh). This serves as a kind of evidence for what precedes it in the words of Allah, the Exalted: "Allah knows..." and so on. ﴿The Great﴾, the one of supreme dignity, to whom everything is inferior. ﴿The Most High﴾, the one who exalts Himself over everything by His power, or the one who is free from the attributes of created things.

After Allah, glorified is He, had explained that He knows all the states of the human being in the stages of his creation, and encompasses both the unseen and the witnessed realms, He explained that He, the Exalted, knows all that they do and all that they leave undone of deeds and words, and that with respect to Him there is no difference between the secret and the openly declared. So He said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 10:

﴿Whether among you one conceals speech⦗ (the word) in his self⦘.

﴿And whoever speaks it aloud⦗ makes it manifest to others⦘.

﴿And whoever is one who hides himself⦗ one who exaggerates in concealment, as if he were hidden⦘.

﴿By night⦗ and seeks increase⦘.

﴿And one who moves freely⦗ from sariba, surūban (to go about openly)⦘.

﴿By day⦗ one who is manifest, whom everyone sees, i.e., one who has come out. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "whoever is hiding himself," or upon "hiding himself." The phrase "man" (whoever) here refers to the two, as in the verse of the poet:

Come, if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, we will be like the two who travel together, O wolf.

As if it were said: "Equal among you are two: one hiding by night, and one moving freely by day." And "equality" (istiwāʾ) is attributed to "whoever conceals" and "whoever speaks aloud," and to "the one hiding himself" and "the one moving freely," but in reality it is attributed to what he conceals and what he speaks aloud, or to the agent insofar as he is an agent, as in the last two. The mention of concealing and hiding first is to show the perfection of God's knowledge; it is as if His knowledge of hidden things precedes His knowledge of apparent things. Otherwise, His relation to all of them is equal, for the reason you have just learned.

﴿For him﴾: that is, for each of those who conceal their speech or declare it openly, and for the one who hides himself, or the one who goes about freely (al-sārib).

﴿Mu'aqqibāt﴾ (successive angels): angels who follow one another in guarding him. It is the plural of mu'aqqiba, from 'aqqabahu, an intensive form of 'aqaba, meaning "to come after someone's heels." It may be that some of them follow others, or that they follow his words and deeds and record them. Or it may derive from i'taqaba, with the tā' assimilated into the qāf, and the tā' then serves as an intensive. Or the intended meaning of al-mu'aqqibāt is "groups." It was also recited as *maʿāqīb*, the plural of *muʿaqqib* or *muʿaqqiba*, with the yā' substituted for one of the two qāfs.

﴿from before him and from behind him﴾: from all his sides, or, in terms of deeds, from what he has put forward and what he has delayed.

﴿They guard him by the command of Allah﴾: from His punishment when he sins, by granting him respite and by seeking forgiveness on his behalf. Or they guard him from harms. Or they watch over his circumstances by the command of Allah, exalted is He. This has also been recited with the word *bi*. It has been said that *min* here means *bi*, and that *min amri Allah* is a second description of *mu'aqqibāt*. It has also been said that the mu'aqqibāt are the guards and the henchmen around the ruler who guard him against what he imagines might be the decree of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not change a favour upon a people﴾ from blessing and well-being ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾ of righteous deeds, or of the dispositions that are the natural disposition (fiṭra) of Allah, upon which He created people, into their opposites. ﴿And when Allah intends harm for a people﴾ because of their bad choice and their deserving of it ﴿there is no repelling it﴾, so there is no averting it. The element governing *idhā* is what the response clause indicates.

﴿And they have no protector other than Him﴾ who takes charge of their affairs and repels from them the evil that Allah has willed for them, because of what their hands have done in changing what is within them. This indicates that the non-fulfilment of His will, exalted is He, is impossible. It also gives notice that they, by what they have engaged in, namely denial of resurrection, hastening evil, and demanding a sign, have changed what is in themselves of the natural disposition. For this they deserved the descent of Allah's anger and His punishment, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 12:

﴿He it is who shows you the lightning, [as] fear﴾ of the thunderbolt, ﴿and [as] hope﴾ for the rain. The reason for placing fear before hope is evident, since what is feared for is one's self or the wealth at hand, while what is hoped for is wealth awaited. It has been said: the fear is also of the rain, but the one who fears it is not the one who hopes for it, such as the potter and the farmer. The sequence [of the words] rejects this, unless one forces the meaning to what has been indicated, namely that what is feared is at hand, while what is hoped for is awaited. As for the case of [the two words] ﴿fear﴾ and ﴿hope﴾: either they are in the verbal-noun form (al-masdariyya), i.e. "you fear a fear and you hope a hope," or they are in the circumstantial form (al-haaliyya) from the lightning, or from the addressees with the implied ﴿possessors (dhawi)﴾, or by making the verbal noun carry the sense of the passive participle, or the active participle for emphasis, or in the causative form (al-'illiyya), by supposing an omitted noun, i.e. "for the sake of [the] inspiring of fear and hope." Or by interpreting it as "causing fear" and "causing hope," so that the agent of the cause and the agent of the caused action are one. As for making the thing caused be the seeing that is implied by the intention, following the manner of the saying of al-Nabigha:

Ḥallat buyūtī fī yafā'in mumamna'in
takhālu bihi rā'iya al-ḥamūlati ṭā'iran

Ḥiḏāran 'alā an lā yunāla mu'āwinī
wa lā niswatī ḥattā yamutna ḥarā'iran

That is: "I placed my houses on a fortified height, on which one would think the shepherd of the camel-caravan is a bird, out of caution, lest my helper be harmed, nor my women, until they die free." That is, "I settled my houses out of caution," so there is no way to it, because what occurs in the position of a remote cause, especially fear, is not suitable as the cause of their seeing.

﴿And He produces the clouds﴾, the clouds drawn along in the air, ﴿the heavy﴾ with water. The word is the plural of ﴿thaqīla﴾ (heavy), and the clouds are described by it because the collective noun (ism jins) carries the sense of a plural, and its singular is ﴿saḥāba﴾. It is said: ﴿saḥāba thaqīla﴾ (a heavy cloud) and ﴿saḥāb thiqāl﴾ (heavy clouds), just as it is said: ﴿imra'a karīma﴾ (a noble woman) and ﴿niswa kirām﴾ (noble women).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 13, verse 13:**

﴿And the thunder glorifies [Him] with His praise﴾, i.e., those among the servants who hear it, who hope for rain, are engaged in praising Him, crying out "Glory be to Allah" and "Praise be to Allah." Attributing the glorification to the thunder is because it prompts them to do so. Or, the thunder itself glorifies Him, on the basis that its glorification is an expression of its indication of His Oneness, exalted be He, and of His bounty, which warrants praise for Him.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he used to say: "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise." And when it grew intense, he would say: "O Allah, do not kill us with Your anger, do not destroy us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that." It is reported from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Glory be to the One to whom it has glorified." And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "The Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the thunder, and he said: 'It is an angel from among the angels, appointed over the clouds, with whips of fire (p-10) with which he drives the clouds.'" And it is reported from al-Hasan: "It is a creature from among the creatures of Allah, Exalted be He, and is not an angel."

﴿And the angels﴾, i.e., the angels glorify [Him] ﴿out of fear of Him﴾, out of awe of His majesty, and of His exalted glory. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the thunder.

﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾, destroying him thereby. ﴿And they﴾, i.e., the disbelievers addressed in the Exalted words: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾. The address has shifted to the third person (ghaybah, shift from direct address to third-person reference), as a notice of their being dropped from the rank of being addressed, a turning away from them, and an enumeration of their crimes before everyone who deserves to be addressed. It is as if it were said: "He is the One who performs such wondrous acts as showing the lightning, producing the heavy clouds, and sending the thunderbolts, which indicate the perfection of His knowledge and power, and which are understood by whoever among the believers understands them." Or [the pronoun refers to] the thunder itself, or the angel appointed over it, and the angels. [They] act in accordance with what this requires: glorification, praise, and fear of His exalted majesty. And [the] disbelievers, whose misdeeds have been related, [are] with their abjectness, their humiliation, and the meanness of their station.

﴿They dispute concerning Allah﴾, i.e., concerning His affairs, Exalted be He, in that they do what they do: denying the Resurrection, hastening the punishment mockingly, and demanding signs. The waw (و, "and") here is for conjoining the sentence to what precedes it, namely the Exalted words: "It is He who shows you the lightning..." etc., or to His words: "Allah knows what every female bears..." etc. As for conjoining it to His words: "And those who disbelieve say..." as has been said, there is no room for that, because His words: "Allah knows..." etc. are a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a sentence beginning a new thought) explaining the falsity of their saying that, and its counterparts such as hastening the punishment and denying the Resurrection, which cuts off the conjunction of what follows to what precedes it.

It has also been said that the phrase is circumstantial (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject), meaning: "He strikes with the thunderbolts whom He wills, while they are in dispute." And it has been said that this refers to what befell Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, the brother of Labid, when he came, together with 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intending to harm him. They entered the mosque while he, peace and blessings be upon him, was sitting in a group of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). They were struck by the beauty of 'Amir, who was one of the most handsome of men. 'Amir had instructed Arbad: "When you see me speaking to Muhammad (ﷺ), go around behind him and strike him with the sword." So he began speaking to him (ﷺ), and Arbad went around behind him (ﷺ) and drew a span of his sword, but Allah held him back, so he could not draw it out completely, while 'Amir gestured to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) saw the situation and said: "O Allah, suffice me against them both however You will." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent a thunderbolt upon Arbad on a clear, scorching day, and it burned him. 'Amir fled, and took refuge in the house of a Salulite woman. When morning came, he buckled on his weapons, his color changed, and he mounted his horse and began to gallop in the desert, saying: "Come forth, O Angel of Death," and reciting poetry, saying: "By al-Lat, if Muhammad and his companion appear to me, meaning the Angel of Death, I will pierce them both with my spear." So Allah sent an angel who struck him with his wing, throwing him down into the dust, and immediately a great swelling came out on his knee. He returned to the house of the Salulite woman saying: "A swelling like the swelling of a camel, and death in the house of a Salulite woman!" Then he called for his horse, mounted it, and ran it until he died upon its back.

It has also been said that what is meant is what is reported from al-Hasan: "There was a man, one of the tyrants of the Arabs. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent a group of his Companions to call him to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He said to them: 'Tell me about what you call me to: what is it, and of what is it made? Is it of gold, or of silver, or of copper, or of iron, or of pearls?' They were appalled at his speech, and returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'We have not seen a man with a more disbelieving heart, nor more defiant toward Allah than him.' He (ﷺ) said: 'Return to him.' They returned to him, but he only increased in his first saying, and in its wickedness. So they returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of what he had done, and he (ﷺ) said: 'Return to him.' They returned, and while they were with him, disputing with him, a cloud rose up, thundered, flashed, and hurled a thunderbolt, and the disbeliever was burned. They came running to inform the Prophet (ﷺ) of the news, and the Companions met them. They said: 'Your companion has been burned.' They said: 'How did you know?' They said: 'It was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ).'"

﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾, i.e., and the state is that He is severe in His contention, in His might, and in His stratagem against His enemies, when He plots against them and exposes them to destruction. From this comes "tamahhala" (he exerted himself), when he undertook to use stratagems. It has also been said that the word (mihal, "strength/stratagem") is derived from (mahl, "strength"), meaning "power." It has also been said that it is transformed from (hawl, "power/stratagem") or (hilah, "trick"), and was made into a weak letter contrary to analogy. What supports this is that it has been read with the mim vowelled with a fatha, as a form of the pattern (maf'al) from (hala yahulu), meaning "he devised a stratagem." It may also be that it means "the backbone," so that it becomes a proverb for strength and power, like their saying: "The arm of Allah is stronger, and His cutting edge is sharper."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 14:

﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾. That is: the call that is established, that is in its proper place, and that is answered when it is made. The idafa (genitive construction, "the call of truth") is to indicate its association with the truth, its being specific to it, and its being far removed from any trace of falsehood, loss and error, just as one says "a word of truth" (kalimat al-haqq). It has also been said that "to Him is the call" means the call of God, glorified is He, that is: the call that is fitting to His presence, as in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever's migration was to God and His Messenger, his migration is to God and His Messenger." The mention of the attribute of truth is to nurture the meaning of response. The better view is the first, because of His saying, exalted is He: "And the call of the disbelievers is only in error." The connection of the two sentences with what precedes them is that the destruction of Arbad and Amir is impossible from God, exalted is He, and is a response to the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) against them, if the verse was revealed concerning them; or in that it is a threat to the disbelievers for disputing with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by the descent of what is impossible for them, and a warning to them that his supplication against them will be answered.

﴿And those who call upon﴾, that is: the idols, whom the polytheists call upon, the relative pronoun being omitted, ﴿besides Him﴾, besides God, mighty and majestic, ﴿do not respond to them with anything﴾ of their requests ﴿except like one who stretches out his hands toward water﴾. That is: except a response of the kind that the response of water is to one who stretches out his hands toward it from afar. So the word "response" (istijabah) is a verbal noun from the active form, according to what the apparent verb requires, namely "they do not respond"; and it may also be a verbal noun from the passive form. It is construed with "the one who stretches out" on the basis that the verbal noun from the active form entails the verbal noun from the passive form, in existence and in non-existence. So it is as if it were said: they do not respond to them with anything, so nothing is responded to for them except a response of the kind, like the response of one who stretches his hands toward water, as in the saying:

"Misfortune of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth nothing but the stripped or the scraped."

That is: it has left, so there remains nothing but the stripped or the scraped.

﴿That he may reach﴾, that is: the water by itself, without being taken up by anything from a vessel or the like, ﴿his mouth; but it will not reach it﴾, that is: the water will never reach it, because it is inanimate and does not perceive his thirst nor his stretching out of his hand toward it, much less has the capacity for what he intends of "reaching" his mouth. He has likened the state of the polytheists, in that they achieve nothing whatsoever in calling upon their gods, and the feebleness of their opinion in this, to the state of a thirsty, bewildered man who does not know what he is doing, who has stretched out his hands from afar toward water, seeking that it reach his mouth, without regard to the likeness in every detail of the parts. For water in itself is something beneficial, unlike their gods. The meaning is the negation of response entirely, but the speech has been brought out in the form of mockery toward them, so it is said: they do not respond to them with any response except a response in this form, which has in it no trace of response at all; so it is in reality of the type of suspension upon the impossible. It has been read: "tad'una" (you call) with the ta', and "kabasit" with tanwin.

﴿And the call of the disbelievers is only in error﴾, that is: in going astray, perishing and loss.

﴿And to Allah﴾ alone ﴿prostrates﴾, meaning submits and yields, to nothing else, neither independently nor in partnership. Thus the restriction (qasr) encompasses both reversal (qalb) and singling out (ifrad).

﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ of the angels and the two weighty ones (the jinn and mankind).

﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾ meaning: willing ones and unwilling ones. Or, submission of willingness and unwillingness. Or, a state of willingness and unwillingness. For the submission of all to the majesty of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and their yielding to the bringing into being of what He wills for them of the rulings of creation and annihilation, whether they wish it or refuse. And the absence of any intrusion of another's judgment, or even of a judgment other than His, Exalted, in those affairs is something that is not hidden from anyone.

﴿and their shadows﴾ meaning: and the shadows of those among them who have shadows yield to Him, Exalted, namely humans, in that they are disposed according to His will and are subject to His purpose in lengthening, shortening, shifting and vanishing.

﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) of the implied prostration, or a circumstantial clause (hal) of the shadows. The specifying of the two times by mention, although their submission is realized at all times of their existence, is because it is most evident at these two times. Al-ghuduww is the plural of ghadah, like fatiyy is the plural of fatah. Al-asal is the plural of asil, and it is said: it is the plural of asl, and asil is what lies between the afternoon prayer and sunset. It is also said: al-ghuduww is a verbal noun, and what supports this is that it was read as (wal-iySal), meaning entering the evening. This being said, it has been said that the intended meaning is the actual prostration, since the disbelievers in a state of necessity [prostrate to Allah], and this is what is meant by the saying of the Exalted: "and unwillingly they single Him out for prostration," [i.e., the Exalted's words] ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾. It is not far-fetched that Allah, Exalted, may create in the shadows understandings and intellects by which they prostrate to Allah, Glorified be He, just as He created them for the mountains until they became occupied with glorifying Him, and signs of manifestation appeared in them, as Ibn al-Anbari said. It is also permissible that their prostration be understood as what is observed in them of the form of prostration following their owners. You know well that restricting the prostration of the disbeliever in a state of necessity and hardship to Allah, Glorified be He, is of no benefit, for their prostration to their idols in a state of ease undermines the restriction derived from the fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa al-majrur). So the correct view is to take prostration as submission, and because realizing the submission of all in origination and annihilation to Him, Exalted, is more fitting as a rebuke against taking protectors besides Him than realizing their prostration to Him, Exalted. The mention of the submission of rational beings specifically, although others are likewise, is because they are the principal element, and their submission is evidence of the submission of others. On this point He clarified it with His saying, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?﴾ This is to establish that the Creator of both, the one who manages their affairs together with everything in them without exception, is God, glorified is He. His words, exalted is He, ﴿Say: God﴾, are a command to give the answer from the Prophet (ﷺ), indicating that he is the one who must give it, so that he and the opponent are equal in affirming it. Or it is a command to report their acknowledgment, as a notification that they must do so, as if it were said: Relate their acknowledgment, then rebuke them with what binds them to the proof, and silence them. Or it is a command to prompt them with the answer if they falter in replying, out of fear of being bound by it, for they will not be able to restrain themselves at that point and will not be able to deny it. ﴿Say﴾ is for binding them and rebuking them. ﴿Have you then taken﴾ for yourselves, the hamza (همزة, the interrogative particle) here is for denying the reality of the event, as in your saying: أضَرَبْتَ أباكَ (did you strike your father?), not for denying that the event occurred, as in your saying: أضَرَبْتَ أبِي (did you strike my father?). The fa' (فاء, the conjunction) is for coordination with an implied clause after the hamza, meaning: Did you know that their Lord is God, the one to whose command all who are in them submit entirely, and then take, after that, ...

﴿Apart from Him, protectors﴾ who are powerless.

﴿who possess not for themselves any benefit﴾ that they might bring about, ﴿nor any harm﴾ that they might ward off from themselves, let alone having power to bring benefit to others or ward off harm from them. The negation is not directed at both conjoined items together, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ when the conjoined item is taken as ﴿Will you not then hear?﴾. Rather it is directed at the sequence of the second upon the first, together with the necessity that its opposite follow from it, as when one supposes: ﴿Will you then hear?﴾. The meaning is: After you have known that their Lord is God, mighty in majesty, have you taken, apart from Him, powerless protectors, when the requirement of knowing this is only to restrict oneself to His guardianship? Yet you have reversed the matter, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿He was of the jinn and he defied the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his offspring as protectors apart from Me?﴾. Here He described the protectors by lacking the ownership of benefit and harm in order to reinforce and emphasise the denial, just as the taking there was restricted by the circumstantial clause, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿and they are an enemy to you﴾. Each of these negates the taking mentioned and reinforces its denial. ﴿Say﴾ depicts their feeble opinions in the form of something perceptible.

﴿Is the blind man equal﴾ who is the polytheist ignorant of worship and of who deserves it,

﴿and the seeing man﴾ who is the monotheist (tawhid, affirmation of God's oneness) who knows this? Or the first refers to the worshipped one who is heedless, and the second is an indication of the worshipped one who knows everything.

﴿Or are the darknesses equal﴾ which are an expression of disbelief and misguidance,

﴿and the light﴾ which is an expression of monotheism and faith. It was also read with the yā' (ياء, the letter yā') as يَسْتَوِي. Since the noble composition indicates that the disbelief in what they did, in taking idols as protectors apart from God, glorified is He, is pure error and utter mistake, such that its falsity is not hidden from anyone, and that they in this are like the blind man who is guided to nothing at all, and that they have no doubt that could be a source of their error and mistake, let alone a proof, this was emphasised and it was said:

﴿Or have they made for God﴾ i.e., rather have they made for Him ﴿partners who created as He created﴾, glorified is He. The hamza here is for denying the occurrence, not for denying the reality while it occurs. His words, ﴿who created as He created﴾, are what the denial is directed at; as for the act of making itself, it is an occurred reality to which the denial does not attach in this sense. The meaning is: they did not make for God, exalted is He, partners who created as He created, ﴿so that the creation became confused for them﴾ because of that, and they said: these created as God, exalted is He, created, so they deserved worship as He deserves it, that being a source of their mistake. Rather, they made for Him partners who are far removed from that entirely. In this is what is not hidden of allusion to the feebleness of their opinion and mockery of them.

﴿Say﴾ to establish the truth and to guide them to it: ﴿God is the Creator of everything﴾ wholly, there is no creator besides Him, so that He would share with Him in the right to be worshipped.

﴿And He is the One﴾ who is singular in divinity, unique in lordship,

﴿the Subduer﴾ over everything other than Him. How then can it be imagined that He has a partner? And after the polytheist and polytheism were likened to the blind man and the darknesses, and the one who affirms God's oneness and affirmation of oneness were likened to the seeing man and the light, the Truth, which is the Great Qur'an, was likened in its outpouring from the sacred presence upon hearts empty of it and varying in readiness, and in its flowing over them through observance and preservation, and on the tongues through remembrance and recitation, and in its remaining in them while it sustains their spiritual life and the noble qualities and pleasing deeds that follow it, to water sent down from heaven that flows in dry valleys whose customs did not include that, a flow measured by a quantity required by wisdom for the revival of the earth and what is upon it, the remainder remaining in it according to what the benefits of people revolve around. And in its being an adornment with which souls adorn themselves and reach everlasting joy, and a provision enjoyed in livelihood and in the hereafter, like gold, silver, and the rest of the metals from which various kinds of tools and implements are made, which remain useful for a long time. And the falsehood with which the disbelievers were afflicted, owing to the shortness of their view, was likened to what appears on them without any mixing of it into them, and without any disturbance of their clarity, namely the foam rising above them, which quickly vanishes. Then it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 17:

(p-14)﴿He sent down from the sky﴾, i.e., from its direction.

﴿water﴾, i.e., much of it, or a kind of it; namely, rainwater.

﴿So the valleys flowed﴾ with it, ﴿valleys﴾ situated in their places, not all valleys, since rains do not cover all regions. It is the plural of wadi (wadi, a valley), which is an open space between mountains, or hills, or sand dunes, in an irregular plural form, like nad and andiyah (a gathering place and its plural), and naj and anjiyah (a secret conversation and its plural). They said: The reason is that fa'il comes in the meaning of fa'il (fa'il in the sense of fa'il/fa'il): like nasir and nasir, shahid and shahid, alim and alim. Since fa'il was pluralized as af'ilah, as in jarib and ajribah, fa'il was also pluralized as af'ilah. If by them is meant what flows in them, metaphorically, then the attribution of flowing to them is literal; and if their literal meaning is intended, then the attribution is metaphorical, as in "the river flowed." The choice of this image over permanently flowing rivers is because of the clear similarity between their state and the state of what is compared with them, as has been pointed out. ﴿according to their measure﴾, i.e., they flowed carrying their measure which Allah Almighty determined and which His wisdom required for the benefit of people; or according to their measure, which varies in quantity and abundance, in accordance with the variation of their places in smallness and largeness. Not by their being filled and covered by it, but merely by their smallness, which implies the scarcity of water sources, and their largeness, which requires the abundance of sources; for the source of a torrent flowing in a small valley is less than the source of a torrent flowing in a large valley. This is if by the valleys is meant what flows in them. As for if their literal meaning is intended, then the meaning is: their waters flowed according to the measure of those valleys, in the manner you have just understood; or by their pronoun is meant their waters, by way of istikhdam (a figure where one word carries two meanings), and by their measure is meant what was mentioned first of the two meanings. ﴿So the flood carried﴾ flowing in those valleys, i.e., it bore with it ﴿foam﴾, i.e., scum and froth. That was described by His saying ﴿rising﴾, i.e., high and swelling above it, explaining what is meant by the carrying, which is for the carried thing not to float, like heavy trees. The carrying was not averted by saying "the flood carried above it" in order to indicate that that being above is the requirement of the nature of foam, not from the side of what is carried, to establish the similarity between it and what was compared to it, namely falsehood, whose nature is to appear at first glance without entering into the truth.

﴿And from that which they heat in the fire﴾, i.e., they perform the heating upon it while it is in the fire. The pronoun refers to people, and it is left implicit though not previously mentioned, because it is evident. It was read with the second-person form.

﴿seeking ornament or utensils﴾, i.e., for the purpose of making an ornament, which is what is adorned and beautified with, like ornaments made of gold and silver; or making utensils, which is what is enjoyed, such as vessels and tools made of lead, iron, and other metals.

﴿Foam﴾ is dross, ﴿like it﴾, like what was mentioned of the foam of water in being high above it. So His saying "foam" is a subject, and its predicate is the fronted adverbial phrase; "min" is for beginning, indicating merely that it is a subject and originates from it. "Li" is partitive, expressing that it is a part of it, as was said, because that would disrupt the comparison. Expressing it by the relative pronoun, and addressing what is within the relative clause of heating the fire upon it, follows the customs of majesty by showing disdain for it, as in His saying: ﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, upon the clay﴾. It also indicates how the foam comes from it by its melting. The addition of "in the fire" indicates exaggeration in the effort to melt it and the occurrence of foam as noted. And there is no mention of its extraction from (p-15)the earth, because that aspect has no role in the comparison, just as the aspect of sending down water from the sky has a role in it, as detailed previously; rather, it would disrupt that.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that wondrous manner containing exquisite points, ﴿Allah strikes the truth and falsehood﴾, i.e., the parable of truth and the parable of falsehood. The omission is to indicate complete correspondence between the one compared and the one to which it is compared, as if the parable presented were itself the truth and falsehood. After establishing the comparison, along with hints in its folds to the aspects of similarity in the most wondrous and delightful ways, as has been pointed out in their places, He explained the outcome of each of the two compared things in the manner of the comparison, with explicit mention of some of what makes the similarity, namely passing away and remaining, to complete the purpose of the comparison: urging the following of the established truth and deterring from the transient falsehood. So it was said: ﴿As for the foam﴾ of each of them, ﴿it passes away as scum﴾, i.e., cast away. It was also read as (jufalan), and the meaning is one. ﴿And as for what benefits people﴾ of them, like pure water and the specific metal, ﴿it remains in the earth﴾. As for water: some of it remains in its benefits, and some of it runs through the veins of the earth to springs, qanawat (underground channels), and wells. As for metal: some of it is shaped into various kinds of ornaments, and some of it is made into kinds of tools and implements. Thus people benefit from each of these in various kinds of benefits for a long period. So the meaning of "remaining in the earth" is more general than remaining in itself, including staying in the hands of those who turn about in it. The order of the wrapping, which occurs in the summary, was changed to agree with the order in the comparison, in consideration of the harmony between the two states of passing away and remaining, and between their mention, since what is considered is the remaining of what remains after the departure of what departs, not before it. ﴿Thus Allah strikes﴾, i.e., like that wondrous striking, ﴿the parables﴾ are struck in every field, to show perfect kindness and care in guidance and direction. This contains an exaltation of the status of this parable and an emphasis on His saying "thus Allah strikes the truth and falsehood," either by considering that this is built upon the first parable, or by making "that" refer to both together. Having explained the condition of each of truth and falsehood, in state and outcome, in the most complete explanation, He began to explain the condition of the people of each of them in outcome, to complete the call through encouragement and warning, so it was said:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 13, Verse 18:**

﴿For those who respond to their Lord﴾ when He calls them to the truth through the various methods of invitation, among which is the coining of parables, for it is the most gentle means of making hearts that are dull understand, and the most powerful way of subduing proud souls. How could it be otherwise, when it portrays the intelligible in the form of the perceptible, and brings forth rare meanings in the guise of the familiar? So what invitation is more deserving than this of response and acceptance? ﴿The best [reward]﴾, that is, the best reward, which is Paradise. ﴿But as for those who do not respond to Him﴾, and who obstinately oppose the manifest truth, ﴿even if they had all that is in the earth﴾ of every kind of wealth, ﴿all of it﴾, such that not a single part of it is missing from its regions, or [had it] gathered and not dispersed over the ages, ﴿and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom﴾, that is, with what is in the earth, and its like with it, all together, in order to free themselves from what befalls them. In this there is a terror of what they will meet that speech cannot encompass.

Grammatically, the relative phrase (al-mawsul, "those who") is the subject (mubtada'), and the conditional clause (al-shartiyyah, "even if...") is its predicate (khabar). However, it is not that the conditional clause was placed in the position of "the evil [reward]" (al-saw'a), so that it stands in opposition to "the best" (al-husna) in the first half, for the sake of the elegance of the antithesis, such that it is as if it were said: "and for those who do not respond to Him is the evil [reward]," as this might suggest. For although the conditional clause indicates the complete wretchedness of their state, it is far from standing in the place of the word "evil" (al-saw'a) accompanied by the lam that enters upon the relative phrase or its pronoun. Upon this the attainment of the aim depends. What actually occurs in that antithesis is "the evil of the reckoning" (su' al-hisab) in the words of the Exalted: ﴿They shall have the evil of the reckoning﴾. Since the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) that serves as the subject in this sentence refers to the relative phrase that serves as the subject in the preceding sentence, its predicate, namely the adverbial clause (al-jumlah al-zarfiyyah), is in reality a predicate of the relative phrase, and it explains the vagueness of the content of the conditional clause that was first given as the predicate of the relative phrase. For this reason the conjunction was omitted, so it is as if it were said: "and those who do not respond to Him, for them is the evil of the reckoning." This is equivalent to saying: "and for those who do not respond to Him is the evil of the reckoning," with added emphasis. Thus the elegance of the antithesis is complete in the most eloquent and most emphatic manner. Then the outcome of this is explained, so it is said: ﴿And their abode is Hell﴾, that is, their place of return. In this there is a kind of emphasis on the interpretation of "the best" as Paradise. ﴿And wretched is the resting-place﴾, that is, the place of settling, and the object of blame is omitted.

It has also been said that the lam in the Exalted's words ﴿For those who respond to their Lord﴾ is connected to His words "Allah strikes the parables," meaning the parables that preceded. And His words "the best" are an adjective of the verbal noun, meaning: they responded with the best response. His words "and those who do not respond to Him" are conjoined to the first relative phrase. His words "even if they had..." etc. form a resumptive statement, directed to explaining what has been prepared for those who do not respond of punishment. The meaning is: thus does Allah strike parables for the believers who respond and the disbelievers who are obstinate, i.e., these two are the parables of the two groups. And you are aware that the heading of responding or not responding has no connection with what the matter of the parable revolves around. Moreover, the widespread usage is that the lam is applied to the one whose admonition by the parable is intended; "yes," [this] may also be used in this sense, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah strikes a parable for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh﴾, and its like. Furthermore, some of the parables that are struck, especially the last parable that is linked to the speech, is not the parable of the two groups, but a parable for truth and falsehood. There is no justification for making the two groups also the ones for whom the parable is struck, by treating it as if it were said: "thus does Allah strike the parables for mankind," for then there would be no reason at all for dividing them into those who respond and those who do not respond. So reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 19:

﴿Is he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ is the Truth (al-haqq) — of the Qur'an, which has been likened to water sent down from the sky and to pure gold (al-ibriz al-khalis) in benefit and usefulness — ﴿the Truth﴾ beyond which there is no truth; or it is the truth to which the parables that were coined point, so that he accepts it, ﴿like one who is blind?﴾ Blindness of the heart, so that he does not witness it, and it is fire upon a mountain (ʿalam). He does not measure its worth, though it is at the highest level of exaltation and greatness. So he remains bewildered in the darkness of ignorance and the abysses of error; or he does not take heed by the parables that have been coined. That is, it is as if he does not know this, except that the intent is to increase the disparagement of his state, so he is described as "the blind." The placing of the fa' after the hamzah (interrogative) serves to direct the denial toward the consequence: the supposition of equivalence arising from the manifestation of the condition of each of the two through the parables coined, and between their destination and their final outcome. It is as if it were said: After the states of each of the two groups have been made clear and their outcomes, the equivalence between them is still imagined. Then it resumes and says: ﴿Only those of understanding will take heed﴾ by what has been mentioned of the reminders, so that they will perceive the disparity and the distance between them. ﴿Those of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾, that is, the pure intellects, free from the sway of habit and the opposition of illusion.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 20:**

﴿Those who fulfill the covenant of Allah﴾, meaning what they bound upon themselves of acknowledging His lordship (rububiyyah), exalted is He, when they said, "Yes" (bala). Or it means what Allah pledged to them in His Books. ﴿And do not break the solemn pact﴾, meaning what they affirmed upon themselves and accepted, such as belief in Allah, and other covenants between them and Allah, and between (p-17) the servants. This is a generalization (ta'mim) after a specification (takhsis), and it contains an emphasis on the continuity (li'l-istimrar) understood from the form of the imperfect verb (al-mustaqbal, the future/imperfect form).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 21:

﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ of the ties of kinship, the allegiance of the believers, and belief in all the prophets, who agreed upon the truth, without distinguishing between any of them. It also includes observing all the rights of people, indeed the rights of everything connected to them, including cats and chickens.

﴿And they fear their Lord﴾ with the fear of His majesty, awe, and dread, so they do not disobey Him in what He has commanded.

﴿And they dread the evil of the reckoning﴾ so they take account of themselves before they are brought to account. This indicates the extent of its severity, as mentioned earlier.

﴿And those who patiently persevere﴾ through everything the self dislikes, of actions and abstentions, ﴿seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾, desiring His pleasure alone, without looking to the side of creation through showing off (riyā') and seeking a reputation (sum'ah), nor to the side of the self through adornment and self-admiration (ujb). Since patience in the manner mentioned is the essence of the matter in all the connections (ṣilāt) mentioned before and after, it is expressed in the past tense form (ṣīghat al-māḍī, صِيغَةِ الماضِي) out of concern for its importance and to indicate that its realization is obligatory. For it is something indispensable, either in the connections themselves, as in those other than the first, fourth and fifth, or in the manifestation of their rulings, as in the three connections mentioned. Although they are independent of patience in themselves, since there is no hardship for the self in acknowledging the Lordship (rubūbiyyah), in fear (khashyah) and in dread, nevertheless the manifestation of their rulings and acting in accordance with what they require is not free of need for patience. ﴿And they establish the prayer﴾, the obligatory one, ﴿and spend from what We have provided them﴾, that is, a portion of it, the part they are obligated to spend, ﴿secretly﴾, for one who is not known for wealth, or for one who is not suspected of neglecting zakat, or at the time of spending and giving to one whom dignity prevents from taking openly, ﴿and openly﴾, for one who is not as described, or the first refers to voluntary charity (taṭawwu') and the second to obligatory charity (farḍ).

﴿And they repel evil with good﴾, that is, they repay wrongdoing with kindness, or they follow a good deed with an evil one so that it erases it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: they repel with good speech what comes to them of the evil of others. And from al-Hasan: when they are deprived, they give; when they are wronged, they pardon; when they are cut off, they maintain ties. And from Ibn Kaysan: when they sin, they repent. It was also said: when they see an evil, they command its change. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the object (al-majrūr 'alā al-manṣūb) serves to show the complete concern with good deeds.

﴿Those﴾, who are described with the sublime attributes and the beautiful qualities, is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the adverbial clause (al-jumlah al-ẓarfiyyah), namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for them is the final abode﴾, that is, the outcome of the world, and what the end of its people's affair should be, which is Paradise. It was also said that the prepositional phrase is the predicate of ﴿those﴾, and ﴿the final abode﴾ is the agent of the verb of settling (al-istiqrār). In any case, there is no restriction (qaṣr) in it, so as to raise the objection that some of what is in the connections is not among the obligatory duties (al-'azā'im), whose neglect would prevent one from reaching a good end. The sentence is either the predicate of the coordinated relative clauses, or a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) explaining what they deserved by those attributes, if the coordinated relative clauses are made attributes of "those of understanding" (ulū al-albāb), in the manner of praise, without intending that the mentioned connections have any role in remembrance.

Gardens of Eden (jannatu ʿadn) is in apposition to ʿuqba al-dar (the good end of the abode), or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿they will enter them﴾. ʿAdn means residence (al-iqama). It then became a proper name for one of the gardens, meaning: gardens in which they dwell. It was also said that it is the innermost part of Paradise (butnan al-jannah).

﴿And whoever was righteous among their fathers﴾: "fathers" is the plural of the two parents of each one of them, so it is as if it were said: "among their fathers and their mothers."

﴿And their spouses and their offspring﴾: this is a conjunction (ʿatf) on the nominative pronoun in "they will enter." This is permissible because of the separation by the other pronoun (the ḍamir al-akhar, i.e., the attached pronoun in "them"). Alternatively, it is a direct object of accompaniment (maf'ul maʿahu). The meaning is that He will join to them whoever among their family is righteous, even if such a person does not reach their level of excellence, following them as a mark of honoring their station. This is evidence that rank is raised through intercession, and that those who possess these qualities are brought together with one another, because of the kinship and connection between them in entering Paradise, as an increase in their delight. In the restriction to righteousness (al-salah) there is a cutting off of the vain hopes of one who clings merely to the bond of lineage.

﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾: from the gates of the dwellings, or from the gates of conquests and gifts (al-futuh wa-al-tuhaf), saying:

﴿Peace be upon you﴾ is good news for them of the continuance of safety. ﴿For that you endured﴾ is connected to "upon you," or to something omitted; that is: this great honour is because of your patient endurance, i.e., by reason of your patience, or in return for what you bore of the hardships and toils of patience. The meaning is: if you were weary in the world, you have now found rest. The specification of patience, among the connections mentioned, is because of what we have already put forward: that it has a role in each of them, and an added excellence in that it is the foundation of the matter in each of them, and that none of them is counted of value unless it is for seeking the Face of the Lord, may He be exalted and sanctified. ﴿How excellent is the final abode﴾ means: how excellent is the final abode, which is Paradise. It has been read as "نِعْمَ" with a fatha on the nun, and the original is "نَعْمَ," so the ʿayn is made sukun, sometimes by transferring its vowel to the nun and sometimes without that.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he used to come to the graves of the martyrs at the head of every year and would say: "Peace be upon you for that you endured; how excellent is the final abode."
