Likewise it is related from the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs, may the pleasure of Allah be upon them all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 25:

﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah﴾ is meant to refer to those who oppose the former ones and stubbornly contradict them in adopting the opposites of their qualities.

﴿after its ratification﴾, after they had bound themselves to it through acknowledgment and acceptance, ﴿and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾, namely belief in all the prophets, who agree upon the truth, whereas they believe in some of them and disbelieve in others; and the rights of kinship, the friendship of the believers, and other things, of the matters counted above, whose rights they do not observe. The reason why it did not explicitly mention the negation of fear and dread from them is the indication of "breaking" and "severing" upon that. As for not addressing the negation of the aforementioned patience, it is because its realization was considered within the counted good deeds, so that they would be counted among them; therefore there is no basis for negating it from one whose distance from good deeds is that of the two easts. Likewise, there is no basis for negating prayer and almsgiving from one who does not even circle around the root of faith in Allah the Exalted, let alone the branches of the laws. And if by spending is meant voluntary charity, then its negation falls under severing what Allah the Exalted has commanded to be joined. As for repelling evil with good, its negation from them is evident from what preceded and what follows. For whoever repays the goodness of the Mighty and Majestic with breaking the covenant and opposing the command, and engages in corruption, [is one whose case is as His saying, Exalted is He, describes:] ﴿and they cause corruption on earth﴾, that is: through injustice and the stirring up of strife. How can it be conceived that he repays evil with good, given that it would indicate that he has a part in leading to the punishment which His saying, Exalted is He, reports: ﴿Those﴾ ... etc.? That is: those described with what has been mentioned of the ugly deeds, ﴿for them﴾ because of that ﴿is the curse﴾, that is: removal from the mercy of Allah Exalted, ﴿and for them﴾ along with that ﴿is the evil abode﴾, that is: the evil outcome of the world, or the torment of Hell, for it is their abode. This is because the arrangement of the ruling upon the relative clause indicates the causality of the relative clause for it; and it is not hidden that it has no part in that according to most of the exegetes. For repaying an evil deed with its like is permitted, and repelling bad speech with good; likewise giving when denied, pardoning when wronged, and joining when severed, leaving it does not produce any consequence. As for what has been considered as included under the second relative clause, namely the neglect of some recommended rights, there is no harm in that, because its consideration is from the standpoint that it is among the consequences of neglecting the obligatory duties, by disbelief in some prophets, disobedience to parents, and abandoning the rest of the obligatory rights. And the repetition of "for them" is for emphasis, and to signal the difference between the two and the independence of each of them in being established.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 26:

﴿Allah extends provision﴾ i.e., He makes it abundant ﴿for whomever He wills﴾ of His servants, ﴿and restricts﴾ i.e., He constricts it for whomever He wills, according to what wisdom requires, without anyone having any role in that, nor any awareness of its wisdom. Thus He may extend it to the disbelievers as a respite and gradual enticement (istidraj), and He may constrict it for the believer to increase his reward. So the believer should not be deceived by the expansion of the disbeliever's provision, just as the believer should not despair because of his own restriction.

﴿And they rejoiced﴾ i.e., the people of Makkah rejoiced with the joy of exultation and insolence, not the joy of gladness at the bounty of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿in the life of this world﴾ and in the blessings of it that were extended to them ﴿Yet the life of this world﴾ and what follows it of blessings ﴿in the Hereafter﴾ i.e., in comparison with the blessings of the Hereafter ﴿is but a brief enjoyment﴾ i.e., only a meager thing enjoyed, like the hasty provision of a rider or the provisions of a shepherd. The meaning is: they were content with their portion of this world, turning away from the blessings of the Hereafter, while what they exulted in, compared with what they turned away from, is a little thing of little benefit and swift to vanish.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 27:

﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾, that is, the people of Makkah. The choice of this manner of reference over a pronoun, even though their intended subject is clear from the mention of their rejoicing in the worldly life just before, serves to censure them and to record their disbelief against them. This is what is related of their saying: ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾ This is at the furthest extreme of arrogance and obstinacy, as though the great and dazzling signs that were sent down upon him, peace be upon him, were not signs at all, so that they proposed what wisdom does not require of sensible signs, after which no one has any capacity left to refuse acceptance. For this reason, the answer was commanded with the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills﴾. His leading astray is a will that follows wisdom, the wisdom that calls for it. That is, He creates misguidance in him, by turning his choice toward acquiring it, and leaves him immersed in it, knowing that divine kindness (lutf) will not benefit him and guidance will not profit him, like one who has your character in obstinacy, stubbornness, hardness of disposition, and extremism in corruption, so there is no path for him to guidance. And even if every sign came to him, ﴿and He guides to Himself﴾, that is, to His exalted and great presence, with a guidance that brings one to Him, not merely a general indication of what leads to Him, for that is not restricted to those who are guided, and in it is an honour for them beyond description, ﴿whoever turns in repentance﴾, that is, turns toward the truth and reflects upon the various clear proofs that have been revealed. The reality of inabah (turning in repentance) is entering into the state of goodness. The choice of placing it in the relative clause rather than placing the will there is to draw attention to what calls to guidance, rather than merely to His will, and to signal what prompted the first will, namely the obstinacy mentioned, and in this there is an exhortation to the disbelievers to desist from the rebelliousness and stubbornness in which they are. The choice of the past tense form is to hint at guidance being granted in return for a prior turning in repentance, just as the choice of the present tense form in the first relative clause indicates the continuity of the will in line with the continuity of their obstinacy.

"Alladhina amanu" is a substitute (badal) for "man anab." If "guidance" means continuing guidance, the matter is clear, since faith clearly leads to it. If it means bringing guidance about, then "those who believe" means those whose affair has come to faith, as in His saying, ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾, meaning those who arrive at God-consciousness. Otherwise, faith does not lead to guidance itself. Or it is the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: they are those who believe. Or it is in the accusative as an expression of praise.

﴿And their hearts find rest﴾ means they become settled and calm ﴿in the remembrance of God﴾, that is, in His inimitable speech which contains no doubt, as in His saying, ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾, and His saying, ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾. They know that there is nothing greater than it, so they would not propose other signs. The shift to the present tense serves to convey the continuity of tranquillity and its renewal according to the renewal and multiplicity of the signs. ﴿Surely by the remembrance of God alone do hearts find rest﴾, to the exclusion of other things that souls incline toward among worldly matters. This is evident. As for the other miracles, the restriction (qasr) is because they do not produce tranquillity for one who has not witnessed them, unlike the glorious Qur'an. It is a miracle that endures until the Day of Resurrection, which everyone can witness, and by which all hearts find rest. There is also an indication that disbelievers have no hearts, and their hearts are void, since they did not find rest in the remembrance of God Most High and did not count it a sign, though it is the clearest and most dazzling of signs.

It has also been said: their hearts find rest in remembering His mercy and His forgiveness after anxiety and turmoil caused by fear of Him, as in His saying, ﴿Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of God﴾. Or it means by remembering His proofs that indicate His oneness. Or by remembering Him, exalted is He, as intimacy with Him and devotion to Him. So the meaning of "guidance" is its continuance and persistence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 29:

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is a badal (substitute) for "the hearts," by omitting the mudaf (the governed noun, "the hearts of"), as a badal al-kull (substitute of the whole), as indicated; that is, "the hearts of those who believe." In this there is an indication that the human being is essentially the heart. Or it is a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is the supplicatory sentence in the sense of interpretation (ta'wil), namely His saying: ﴿Blessed (tuba) is for them﴾. Or it is the khabar of an implied mubtada', or it is in the accusative on the basis of praise (madh). So "tuba lahum" is a hal (circumstantial accusative) whose governing element is the two verbs, and tuba is a masdar (verbal noun) from taba, like bushra and zulfa. The waw is changed from a ya', as in muqin and musir. Makkawza al-A'rabi read: "tibi li-tasluma al-ya'" (with kasra, and the ya' retained to be kept sound). The meaning is: they have attained good. Its position (mahall) is accusative, like "salaman laka," or nominative on the basis of the inchoative (ibtida'), and although it is indefinite (nakira), it is so because it carries the sense of supplication, like "salamun 'alayka." The reading in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and a good final return (husn ma'ab)﴾ with the accusative and nominative indicates this. The lam in "lahum" is for clarification (bayan), like it in "suqya laka."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 30:

﴿Thus﴾ (i.e., like that) is the example of that great mission, accompanied by this dazzling miracle: ﴿We have sent you to a community before which other communities have passed away﴾, i.e., have gone by, ﴿many communities before it﴾, to whom messengers were sent.

﴿So that you may recite﴾, i.e., read,

﴿to them that which We have revealed to you﴾ of the Book, which is of great station, and [so that you may] guide them to the truth, as a mercy to them. The placing of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) before the object (al-mansub) is by way of ibham (creating suspense), followed by the clarification (bayan), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾. In this there is, beyond doubt, the eager anticipation of the soul for what is to come, and the goodness of its acceptance of it when it arrives upon it. ﴿While they﴾, i.e., while the state of affairs is that they, ﴿disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, the One of far-reaching mercy whose mercy encompasses everything and whose blessing surrounds it. The shift to the explicit name, which points to the attribute of mercy, is because the sending [of messengers] arises from it, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. So they did not esteem Him as He deserves, nor did they thank His blessings, especially that which He bestowed upon them by sending one like you to them and sending down the Qur'an, which is the source of religious and worldly benefits for them. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca, when they were commanded to prostrate and said, "And what is the Most Merciful?" ﴿Say: He is﴾, i.e., the Most Merciful whom you have disbelieved in and denied knowing,

﴿my Lord﴾. The word rabb in origin means tarbiyah (nurturing), which is bringing a thing to its perfection gradually, step by step; then it was applied to Him as an intensive, as with sawm (fasting) and 'adl (justice). It was also said: it is an attribute, i.e., my Creator and the One who brings me to the stages of perfection. Its mention before His saying ﴿There is no god but He﴾, i.e., there is none deserving of worship besides Him, is a reminder that the entitlement to worship is tied to lordship. It was also said: Abu Jahl heard the Prophet ﷺ saying, "O Allah, O Merciful," so he returned to the polytheists and said, "Muhammad calls upon two gods." Then this was revealed, and there was revealed His saying, Exalted is He: "Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful," the verse. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ in all my affairs, especially in seeking victory over you, and upon no one other than Him.

﴿And to Him alone﴾ ﴿is my return﴾, i.e., my repentance. Like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾. He, peace be upon him, was commanded to do this to make clear the excellence of repentance and its measure with Allah, Exalted is He, and that it is the attribute of the prophets; and to urge the disbelievers to turn back from what they are upon in the most eloquent and gentle manner. For he, peace be upon him, though commanded to it while free from any trace of committing a sin that would necessitate it, however small, [it is clear that] their repentance while they are devoted to various kinds of disbelief and sins is absolutely necessary. The word matab has been interpreted as mere return: it was said, "My return and your return," and it was added, "so that He may judge between me and you." It has also been said: "so that He may reward me for my steadfastness in facing you." So reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 31:

﴿وَلَوْ أنَّ قُرْآنًا﴾ That is, a Qur'an (*qur'anan*) of any kind. *Qur'anan* is the noun of *anna*, and its predicate is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿سُيِّرَتْ بِهِ الجِبالُ﴾ ("the mountains were set moving by it"). The answer to *law* ("if") is omitted because the flow of the speech leads directly to it, such that the listener anticipates it from the reciter. The purpose is either to show the great rank of the Noble Qur'an and the corruption of the opinion of the disbelievers, in that they did not esteem its lofty worth and did not count it among the signs, so they demanded other signs like those given to Musa and 'Isa, peace be upon them both. Or the purpose is to show the extremity of their obstinacy and stubbornness and their persistence in error and corruption. The meaning, according to the first view, is: if a Qur'an had the mountains set moving by it, that is, by its being sent down, or by its being recited over them, and they were shaken from their places, as was done to the mountain (*Tur*) for Musa, peace be upon him.

﴿أوْ قُطِّعَتْ بِهِ الأرْضُ﴾ That is, it was split and made into rivers and springs, as was done to the rock when he struck it with his staff, peace be upon him; or it was made into broken pieces. ﴿أوْ كُلِّمَ بِهِ المَوْتى﴾ That is, after the dead were brought to life by its being recited over them, as the dead were brought to life for 'Isa, peace be upon him. Then *that* would be *this* Qur'an, because it is the highest extreme in containing the wonders of the effects of the power of God, exalted is He, and His awe. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿لَوْ أنْزَلْنا هَذا القرآن عَلى جَبَلٍ لَرَأيْتَهُ خاشِعًا مُتَصَدِّعًا مِن خَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of God"). This is not about miraculousness (*i'jaz*), since it has no place in these effects, nor about reminding, warning and frightening, since those are specific to rational beings. Moreover, these effects have no connection to speaking to the dead, and treating the flow of intellect to them would undermine the intended hyperbole. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the subject in the three positions, in accordance with what has passed more than once, is for the purpose of creating suspense and then clarification, to increase the affirmation. For by placing what should be delayed earlier, the soul remains alert and awaiting the delayed element, asking what it is, so that when it arrives it settles in with greater firmness. The word *aw* ("or") in both positions is for preventing the absence of all (*manʿ al-khuluww*), not for preventing the combination (*manʿ al-jamʿ*). Although their demand concerns merely the appearance of such wondrous acts at his hand, peace be upon him, and not their appearance through the Qur'an, nevertheless, since it was founded upon the Qur'an's supposed lack of extraordinary events, the appearance of these acts was attached to it, as an exaggeration in showing that it contains them, and that it is worthy of being the source of every extraordinary event, and as a demonstration of the feebleness of their opinion regarding its lofty status. It is as if it were said: if the appearance of the like of what they demanded were among the requirements of wisdom, then the place of its manifestation would be this Qur'an, which they did not count as a sign. In this there is what is not hidden of the magnification of its glorious status and the description of them with feebleness of mind. ﴿بَلْ لِلَّهِ الأمْرُ جَمِيعًا﴾ That is, to Him belongs the command upon which the sphere of existences turns, in being and non-being. He does what He wills and decides what He desires, in accordance with the profound wisdoms to which He calls. This is a *idrab* (a turning away) from what the conditional sentence contains of the meaning of negation, not in terms of its explicit wording but in terms of its implication and what it entails. That is: if a Qur'an had been subjected to what was mentioned, that would be this Qur'an; but it was not done, rather what is the present state of affairs was done, because the whole command belongs to Him alone. The turning away is therefore not directed at the fact that the command belongs to God, glorified is He, but at what that entails, namely that the state of affairs is as it is, in accordance with what wisdom requires of basing obligation upon testing.

﴿أفَلَمْ يَيْأسِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ That is: did they not know, according to the dialect of Hawazin, or of a people of al-Nakha', or by using *al-yaʾs* ("despair") in the sense of *al-ʿilm* ("knowledge"), since it includes it? This is supported by the reading of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, and a group of the Companions and the Successors, may God be pleased with them. Did they not clarify by way of interpretation? The *fa'* (then) is for conjunction with an implied element, that is: they were heedless of the fact that the whole command belongs to God, exalted is He, so they did not know ﴿أنْ لَوْ يَشاءُ اللَّهُ﴾ (that if God willed), with the pronoun of the matter omitted and *an* lightened, ﴿لَهَدى النّاسَ جَمِيعًا﴾ ("He would have guided all people") by manifesting the like of those great signs. Thus the denial is directed at both conjoined elements together. Or: know that the whole command belongs to God, and then they did not know what that knowledge requires of what was mentioned; this is then directed at the sequence of the conjoined element after the element it is conjoined to, that is: the second knowledge failed to follow the first knowledge. On both assessments, the denial is a denial of occurrence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ألَمْ يَعِدْكم رَبُّكم وعْدًا حَسَنًا﴾ ("Did your Lord not promise you a good promise?"), not a denial of the reality of what has occurred, as in your saying: "Did you not fear God until you disobeyed Him?" Moreover, the locus of the denial is not merely their lack of knowledge of the content of the conditional sentence, but along with their lack of knowledge that its antecedent is not realized, as if it were said: did they not know that God, exalted is He, if He willed their guidance He would have guided them, and that He did not will it? This is because they were wishing that what they demanded of signs would appear, so that they might unite upon faith. On the second assessment: if a Qur'an had had done to it what was detailed of marvels, they would not have believed in it. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَلَوْ أنَّنا نَزَّلْنا إلَيْهِمُ المَلائِكَةَ وكَلَّمَهُمُ المَوْتى﴾ ("Even if We had sent down the angels to them, and the dead had spoken to them") to the end of the verse. Then the turning away is directed at what preceded of their demand, together with their being in obstinacy as explained. That is: therefore they do not have that; rather the command belongs wholly to God; if He wills He brings what they demanded, and if He wills He does not bring it, according to what the call of wisdom requires, without anyone having any dictation over Him or any demand upon Him. *Al-yaʾs* here means *al-qunut* ("despair"), that is: did not those who believed know their state to be such, so that they did not despair of their faith, until they loved the appearance of their demands? Then the denial is directed at the two conjoined elements, or: know that, and then they did not despair of their faith. Then it is directed at the occurrence of the conjoined element after the element it is conjoined to, that is: at the failure of despair to follow the mentioned knowledge. The denial on both assessments is a denial of occurrence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿أفَلا تَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("Will you not fear God?") and its parallels, not a denial of the occurrence of the fact, for their not despairing of it is something that cannot be repelled. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿أنْ لَوْ يَشاءُ اللَّهُ..﴾ ("that if God willed...") etc., is attached to an omitted element, that is: did those who believed not despair of their faith, knowing that if God willed He would have guided all people, and that He did not will that; or [they knew] with *āmanū* ("believed"), that is: did those who believed not despair, that if God willed He would have guided all people, in the sense of: did the believers not despair of their faith, with the content of the conditional sentence, and with the non-realization of its antecedent, which is understood from their obstinacy, as the word *law* indicates; so the description mentioned is among the motivations for denying their despair. It has been said that Abu Jahl and his like said to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him: "If you are a prophet, set your Qur'an to move the mountains away from Makkah, so that it becomes spacious for us, and we may make gardens and plots of land in it. For they were subjected to Dawud, peace be upon him; so you are not lower in God's estimation than he is, if you are a prophet as you claim. Or subject the wind to us by it, as it was subjected to Sulayman, peace be upon him, so that we may trade over it to Syria, for the crossing of the long distance is hard upon us. Or send us by it two men, or three, from among those of our fathers who have died." So it was revealed. On this account, the meaning of cutting the earth is cutting it by travel, and there is then no need for justification in attributing the mentioned wondrous acts to the Qur'an, as was needed in the first two assessments. It is related from al-Farra' that it is attached to what precedes it, from His saying: ﴿وَهم يَكْفُرُونَ بِالرَّحْمَنِ﴾ ("while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful"), and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause, and it in reality indicates the answer. The estimation is: even if a Qur'an had the mountains set moving by it, or the earth cut by it, or the dead spoken to by it, they would still disbelieve in the Most Merciful. The masculine form in *kullima bihi al-mawta* ("the dead were spoken to by it") is for giving precedence to the masculine among the dead over others. ﴿وَلا يَزالُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("And those who disbelieve will not cease") from the people of Makkah ﴿تُصِيبُهم بِما صَنَعُوا﴾ ("will be struck by what they have done"), that is: because of what they have done of disbelief, persistence in it, and not stating it, whether for the purpose of magnifying its gravity or its repugnance. This is an explicit statement of what is implied by the ruling being built upon the relative clause, namely the causal link of the relative clause to it, together with what the form *ṣuniʿ* ("done") indicates of their firm establishment in that.

﴿قارِعَةٌ﴾ ("A calamity") a calamity that strikes them and disturbs and unsettles them, and it is what used to strike them of kinds of afflictions and disasters, from killing, captivity, plunder and despoiling. Placing the prepositional phrase before the agent is for what has passed many times, namely the intention of clarification after ambiguity, for increased affirmation and firmness, together with what it contains of showing that the axis of the striking is from their side, the most prominent of what has prominence.

﴿أوْ تَحُلُّ﴾ ("or it descends") that calamity ﴿قَرِيبًا﴾ ("near"), that is: a near place ﴿مِن دارِهِمْ﴾ ("close to their dwelling"), so they are frightened by it, and its sparks fly to them. The calamity is likened to an enemy advancing upon them, so striking is attributed to it at one time and descending at another, and therefore there is a metaphor by way of implicit comparison (*istiʿara bi-l-kināya*), imagination (*takhyil*), and development (*tarshih*).

﴿حَتّى يَأْتِيَ وعْدُ اللَّهِ﴾ ("until the promise of God comes"), that is: their death, or the Resurrection, for each of these is a decreed promise that cannot be turned back. In this is an indication that what afflicts them at that time of punishment is extremely severe, and that what was mentioned is a small foretaste compared to it. Then this is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُخْلِفُ المِيعادَ﴾ ("Indeed God does not break the appointment"). *Al-mīʿād* means the promise, like *al-mīlād* and *al-mīthāq* in the sense of birth and covenant, and the assurance, since such a thing is impossible for God, glorified is He. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: by the calamity he meant the expeditions (*sarāyā*) that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to send out, and they were between raids, abductions, and frightening by attacks upon them in their homes. Then striking and descending are among their conditions at that time. According to this, His saying, exalted is He, *aw tahullu qariban min darihim* ("or it descends near their dwelling") may be an address to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, meaning by it his descent at al-Hudaybiyya. And by the promise of God is meant what He promised him of the conquest of Makkah.

And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, so I gave respite to those who disbelieved, then I seized them. So how was My retribution!

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on Surah 13 (al-Ra'd), verse 32:

﴿Indeed, messengers before you were mocked﴾ [i.e., many messengers] who passed away before you. ﴿So I gave respite to those who disbelieved﴾ — that is, I left them for a period of time, in security and ease, as a beast is left to graze in pasture. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he encountered from the polytheists of denial and of making demands in a manner of mockery directed at him, and a warning to them. The meaning: this is not specific to you; rather it is a consistent matter, and it was done to many messengers before you. So I granted a delay to those who did that to them. The shift in the relative clause to the description of disbelief is not because those granted respite were other than the mockers, but in order to combine the two attributes — i.e., I granted respite to those who disbelieved together with their mockery, and nothing else. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment﴾ — that is, My punishment of them. And in this is an indication of the extreme severity and dreadfulness of its manner, which is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 33:

﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾, meaning: a watchful guardian, overseeing [it].

﴿over every soul﴾, whoever it may be, ﴿in what it has earned﴾ of good or evil. Nothing of that is hidden from Him, and He recompenses each one for its deeds. He is God, exalted is He. The predicate is omitted, meaning: "is like one who is not such," as a denial of this. The insertion of the fa' (then) directs the denial toward the supposition of likeness, after what is known of what God, exalted is He, did to the mockers: the long respite and the severe seizing. It also follows from the fact that the whole matter belongs to God, exalted is He, and that the guidance of all people is subject to His will, and from the continuous calamities upon the disbelievers until God's promise comes. It is as if it were said: "The matter is so. Is one whose state is this like those who are counted among things, so that you associate [others] with Him?" The denial thus applies to the consequence of the conjoined clause, namely the supposition of likeness, upon the omitted conjoined clause, namely the state of affairs being as mentioned. This is like your saying, "Do you know the truth and yet do not act upon it?", not a denial directed at both conjoined clauses together, as when you say, "Will you not inform him and yet not act upon it?"

God's saying ﴿And they have set up for God associates﴾ is either an independent sentence, brought in to indicate the predicate, or a circumstantial clause, meaning: "Is the One whose attributes are these like what is not so, while they have set up for Him associates, not a single associate?" Or it is conjoined to the predicate, if something suitable for that is supposed, meaning: "Is the One whose state is this not made one [by them], and have they set up for Him associates?" The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to specify His oneness in essence and in name, and to draw attention to His being exclusively deserving of worship, together with the clarification after the ambiguity, by presenting it as a relative clause, to indicate exaltation.

God's saying ﴿Say: Name them﴾ is a rebuke upon a rebuke. It means: "Name them: who are they? And what are their names? Or describe them. And consider: do they have what would make them deserving of worship and worthy of partnership?" ﴿Or will you inform Him﴾, meaning: "Rather, will you inform God ﴿of what He does not know in the earth﴾", meaning: of partners deserving of worship whom God, exalted is He, does not know, and from whom not the weight of an atom is absent in the heavens and the earth. It was also read with lightening (of the doubled letter): ﴿Or with an outward saying﴾, meaning: "Rather, do you name them partners by an outward saying, without its having any meaning or reality?" Like the naming of a black man as Kafur (camphor). Like His saying, exalted is He: "That is their saying from their mouths." These wondrous methods in which this noble verse came are a proclamation that it lies beyond the power of humans and is speech of the Creator of powers and measures. Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds.

﴿Rather, their scheming was made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾. The relative pronoun is placed in the position of the pronoun, as a reproach to them and a recording against them of disbelief.

﴿their scheming﴾: their deception with falsehoods, or their plotting against Islam through their associationism. ﴿And they were averted from the way of God﴾, meaning: from the way of truth, from ṣadda (to turn away) ṣaddan. It was also read with a kasra on the ṣād, by transferring the vowel of the dāl onto it. It was also read with a fatha on it, meaning: they turned people away, or from ṣadda ṣudūdan (to turn away, to be averse).

﴿And whoever God leaves astray﴾, meaning: He creates straying in him through his bad choice, or He forsakes him.

﴿then he has no guide﴾, who would grant him success in guidance.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 34:**

﴿For them is a punishment﴾ that is severe ﴿in the life of this world﴾ through killing, captivity, and all the other calamities that befall them. Indeed, these calamities befall them only as a punishment for their disbelief.

﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe﴾ than that in intensity and duration. ﴿And they have no protector from Allah﴾ from His punishment mentioned, ﴿no guard﴾ who would shield them from it. Here, the first "min" (مِن in مِنَ اللَّهِ) is connected to the meaning of protection (ṣila lil-wiqāyah), and the second "min" (مِن in مِن واقٍ) is extra (mazīdah) for emphasis.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 35:

﴿The likeness of the Garden﴾ i.e., its wondrous description, which is strange like a parable, ﴿that was promised to the God-fearing﴾ who avoid disbelief and sins. It is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted according to Sibawayh (Sībawayh, the early grammarian). That is: in what We have related to you is the likeness of: the Garden. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Beneath it rivers flow﴾ is an explanation of that likeness, on the basis that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the omitted pronoun in the relative clause, referring back to the Garden; that is, [the Garden] which He promised. According to others, it is the predicate, like your saying "The matter of Zayd: people come to him and honour him." Or [it is explained] by the omission of a qualifier: that is, "The likeness of the Garden is a garden in which rivers flow..." etc.

﴿Its fruit﴾, its produce, ﴿is perpetual﴾, never ceasing, ﴿and its shade﴾ likewise. The sun does not abrogate it (lā tansakhuhu, i.e., naskh, cancellation) as it abrogates the shades of this world. ﴿That﴾ Garden, described by what has been mentioned, ﴿is the final outcome of those who have guarded themselves﴾ against disbelief and sins; that is, their ultimate destination and the end of their affair.

﴿And the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾ alone, and in this there is what is not hidden of encouraging the God-fearing and despairing the disbelievers.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 36:**

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾ are the Muslims among the People of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, Ka'b, and their like, and those Christians who believed. They were eighty men: forty in Najran, eight in Yemen, and thirty-two in Abyssinia.

﴿rejoice at what has been sent down to you﴾, since it is the Book promised in the Tawrah (Torah) and the Injil (Gospel).

﴿and among the factions﴾, that is, among their factions, namely their disbelievers who formed alliances against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in enmity, such as Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, al-Sayyid and al-Aqib, the two bishops of Najran, and their followers.

﴿who deny part of it﴾, which refers to the laws that were newly introduced or abrogated (naskh, meaning the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one), not to those that agree with what they had distorted. Otherwise it would have been reproached to them from the outset that the basis of this was nothing but the misdeeds of their own hands. As for what agrees with their books, they did not deny it, even if they did not rejoice in it. It has been said that the first relative pronoun may be taken to mean their general masses, for they too rejoice in it because it confirms their books in general. In that case, the words of the Exalted, "and among the factions..." etc., form a complement, as if it were said: "And among them are those who deny part of it." ﴿Say﴾ as a binding argument against them and a rejection of their denial.

﴿I have only been commanded to worship God and not associate anything with Him﴾, that is, not to associate any thing with Him, or not to commit association with Him. The intended meaning is to restrict the command to worship to God, Exalted is He, not to restrict the command in general to His worship alone. That is: Say, "I have been commanded in what has been sent down to me to worship God and to affirm His oneness." It is evident that you have no way to deny this, since all the prophets and books agree upon it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we worship none but God, and that we associate nothing with Him﴾ (3:64). Then why do you associate ʿUzayr or the Messiah with Him? It is also recited as "wa-la ushriku bihi" with a nominative ending, as a resumption, meaning: "And I do not associate anything with Him."

﴿To Him﴾, to God, Exalted is He, alone, following the aforementioned path of monotheism, or to what I have been commanded of monotheism.

﴿I call﴾ people to nothing other than Him, or to no other thing that the divine Books and the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, did not agree upon. So what is the basis of your denial? ﴿And to Him﴾, to God, Exalted is He, alone, ﴿is my return﴾, my place of return for recompense. Since this conclusive proof was binding upon them and they could find no escape from it, he, peace and blessings be upon him, was commanded to address them with it as a binding argument and a rebuke. Then he began to refute their denial of the subsidiary laws that were revealed initially, or as replacements for the abrogated laws, by explaining the wisdom behind that, saying:

(p-26)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 37:

﴿And thus did We send it down﴾ That is: like what was sent down to you. "Thus" (dhalika) is a reference to the manner (masdar) of "We sent it down," or of "it was sent down to you." Its position is in the accusative as a verbal noun (mafʿul mutlaq, al-masdariyya). That is: like that wondrous sending down, systematized with foundational principles on which there is consensus, and branches diverging into agreement and disagreement, as the requirement of wisdom and benefit dictates. "We sent it down" as ﴿a judgment﴾, a judge who decides matters and events with truth, or one by which judgment is made in the same way. The mention of that title, although some of it is not a ruling, is to instill the obligation of observing it and the necessity of preserving it.

﴿Arabic﴾, translated into the tongue of the Arabs. The mention of this is to point out that this is one of the points of difference with the earlier Scriptures, although this is what wisdom requires, since by it its understanding becomes easy and the perception of its miraculousness is attained, and limiting the sending down to the foundations of religion on which there is consensus, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship Allah...﴾ etc. Its opposite is the mention of following their desires, and the discussion of abrogation and confirmation ("Allah effaces what He wills and confirms," and "for every term there is a Book"), for what is agreed upon cannot conceivably be subject to following and being followed.

﴿And if you follow their desires﴾ which they call you to, from establishing matters contrary to what has been sent down to you of the truth, such as praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis after the change of direction (qibla).

﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ of great station, flowing from that Arabic judgment, or the knowledge of its content.

﴿you will have from Allah﴾ from His mighty presence; the shift from the first person to the third and the mention of the Majestic Name serve to instill awe. Al-Azhari said: He is not a god until He is worshipped, and until He is a creator, a provider, and a governor.

﴿any protector﴾ who will manage your affairs and support you against those who seek to harm you.

﴿or any defender﴾ who will shield you from the places of evil. Since the negation of a helper against the enemy does not necessarily entail the negation of a shield from his harm, the negative particle has been introduced before the conjoined term for emphasis, as in your saying: "I have neither dinar nor dirham," or: "You have from the punishment of Allah no helper or defender." This is for your following their desires; and such severe admonitions are only for cutting off the hopes of the disbelievers and stirring the believers to steadfastness in the religion. The lam in ﴿la-in﴾ is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatta'a), and ﴿ma laka﴾ stands in place of the answers of both the conditional and the oath.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 38:

﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you⁠﴾ many, existing ﴿before you, and We gave them wives and offspring﴾ (p-27) women and children, just as We gave them to you. This is a refutation of what they used to find fault with him (ﷺ) for: marriage and children. Just as they used to say: "What is wrong with this Messenger, that he eats food?" Etc.

﴿And it was not for any messenger⁠﴾ from among them, meaning: it was not valid, nor proper, and it was not within his capacity,

﴿to bring a sign⁠﴾ from what was proposed to him, or a ruling from what was requested of him, ﴿except by permission of Allah⁠﴾ and His will, which is founded upon the wisdoms and interests on which the affairs of creation revolve, especially such great matters as these. The turn to what we have already presented, and to establish the content of the sentence by alluding to the cause.

﴿For every term⁠﴾ meaning: for every period and time among the periods and times.

﴿there is a Book⁠﴾ a specific ruling that is written for the servants, according as wisdom requires, for all the sacred laws aim at reforming their conditions in the beginning and the return. Part of that is that it varies according to the variation of their changing conditions, according to the change of times, like the variation of treatment according to the variation of the conditions of the sick according to the times.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 39:

﴿Allah erases what He wills﴾ i.e., He abrogates (naskh) whatever rulings He wills to abrogate, in accordance with what wisdom requires according to the time.

﴿And establishes﴾ in its place what contains benefit, or leaves it as it is, unabrogated, or establishes whatever He wills to establish absolutely, which is more general than both of these, and includes the (act of) bringing into existence from the beginning. Or He erases from the register of the recording angels (al-hafazah), whose constant occupation is recording every utterance and every deed that is not connected to a reward, and He establishes what remains. Or He erases the evil deeds of the penitent and establishes good deeds in their place. Or He erases a generation (qarn) and establishes others. Or He erases corrupt things from the physical world and establishes existing beings. Or He erases provision and increases it, or erases the term of life (ajal), or (erases) happiness and misery. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Those who hold this view supplicate Allah, exalted is He, that He make them among the happy. This was narrated by Jabir from the Prophet (ﷺ). The most appropriate approach is to generalize both the erasing and the establishing, so that it encompasses everything, and the matters of denial (mawadd al-inkar) enter into this primarily.

It is also read with the doubled letter (tashdid): ﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾, i.e., its origin. It is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), since nothing, of what passes away or what remains, is not written therein as it is.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 40:**

﴿Whether We show you﴾ its origin is ʾin nurikaʾ (إنْ نُرِكَ). The mā (ما) is extra (mazīdah), added to emphasize the meaning of the conditional, and for this reason the nūn (نُونُ التوكيد, the energetic nūn) was attached to the verb. ﴿some of what We promise them﴾, i.e., We have promised them the sending down of punishment upon them. The shift to the present form (muḍāriʿ, the imperfect) is to depict a past situation vividly (ḥikāyat al-ḥāl al-māḍiyah), or it means "We promise them a renewed promise," as the wisdom requires, of warning after warning (inḏār ghibb inḏār). In the expression "some" (al-baʿḍ) there is a symbolic indication (ramz) that only some of the promised ones are intended.

﴿Or We take you back﴾ before that, ﴿then upon you is only the conveyance (al-balāgh)﴾, i.e., the conveying of the rulings of the message in its entirety, not the realization of the content of what you conveyed of the threat, which is part of it. ﴿And upon Us﴾, not upon you, ﴿is the reckoning (al-ḥisāb)﴾, the calling to account for their evil deeds and the taking of them to task for them. That is: however the situation turns out, We either show you some of what We promised them of worldly punishment, or you do not see it, and in either case that is upon Us. Upon you is only the conveyance of the message, so do not concern yourself with what lies beyond that, for We will suffice you for it, and We will complete what We have promised you of victory, and its delay should not vex you, for that is due to hidden wisdoms that We know. Then He consoled his soul, peace be upon him, by the dawning of its signs, and said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 41:

﴿Have they not seen?﴾ It is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari, a question asking the addressee to deny something). The waw is a conjunction joining it to an implied clause that the context requires, meaning: "Did they deny the descent of what We had promised them, or did they doubt it, or did they not reflect upon this, and have they not seen ﴿that We come to the land﴾, that is, the land of disbelief, ﴿reducing it from its extremities﴾, by Our opening it to the Muslims little by little, joining it to the abode of Islam, and removing its people from it through killing, capture, and expulsion? Is this not of that kind?" Similar to it is His saying, exalted is His authority: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its extremities? Are they the victors?﴾ His saying "nanqusuha" (نَنْقُصُها) is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the subject of "na'ti" (نَأْتِي) or from its object. It has also been read as "nunaqqisuha" (نُنَقِّصُها) with the doubled letter (tashdid). In the word "al-ityan" (coming), which indicates the inevitable taking-over and the great seizure, there is a grandeur that is not hidden, as in His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And We will turn to what they had done of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾.

﴿And Allah judges﴾ whatever He wills as He wills. Victory and favour have been decreed for Islam, and humiliation and decline for disbelief, as is observed from the signs and effects. In the shift from the first person (speaking) to the third person (absent), and in building the judgment upon the sublime Name, there is a clear indication of grandeur, the cultivation of awe, and the confirmation of the content of the statement by mentioning the cause. This is an intervening sentence (jumla i'tirawiyya), brought in to emphasise the meaning of what precedes it. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿None can repel His decree﴾ is an intervening clause within an intervening clause, to explain the elevated status of His judgment, glorified is His majesty. It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), as if it were said: "And Allah judges, His judgment being executed," just as you say: "Zayd came, without a turban on his head," meaning, bareheaded. The mu'aqqib (مُعَقِّب, one who repels) is the one who turns back upon a thing and nullifies it. Its root meaning is one who follows it and pursues it with rejection and nullification. From this it is said of the rightful creditor: mu'aqqib, because he pursues his debtor with demand and claim.

﴿And He is swift in reckoning﴾: so before long He will call them to account and requite them in the Hereafter with varied punishments, after what He inflicted upon them through killing, capture, and expulsion, as is seen. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "Swift in retribution."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 42:

﴿And indeed those who were before them plotted﴾ — the disbelievers ﴿who came before them﴾, i.e., before the disbelievers of Makkah, against their prophets, and against the believers, just as these (disbelievers) have plotted. This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that their plotting has no consequence and no effect; rather, it has no real existence at all. He did not state this explicitly, being content with the indication of the restriction (qasr) derived from its causal explanation, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs all plotting﴾, i.e., the entire category of plotting ﴿entirely﴾. Their plotting has no existence at all, since it is the conveying of harm to another from a direction he does not perceive; and since all that they do and all that they leave undone is by the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and His power, they have only mere acquisition (kasb) without any act or effect. This is what His saying, mighty and majestic is He, clarifies: ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾. From the requirement of this is the protection of His friends (awliya') and the punishment of those who plot against them, so that every soul is recompensed for what it has earned. It becomes clear that their plotting, in relation to those against whom they plotted, has neither substance nor effect. And that all plotting belongs to Allah, the Exalted, in that He takes them to account for what they earned of the various kinds of disobedience, of which their plotting is one part, ﴿from where they do not expect﴾. Or it means: ﴿to Allah belongs the plotting﴾ which they all carried out, not to them, in the sense that this is not plotting from them against the prophets, but is in fact plotting from Allah, the Exalted, against them, while they do not perceive it, since ﴿the evil plotting does not encompass anyone except its own people﴾.

﴿And the disbelievers will know﴾ when He judges according to the requirement of His knowledge, and so fully recompenses every soul for what it has earned, ﴿to whom belongs the good end of the abode﴾, i.e., the praiseworthy outcome from both groups, even if they are ignorant of this on that day. It has been said: the sin (sin) is for emphasizing the certainty of that occurring and their knowledge of it at that time. It has also been read: (sa-ya'lamu al-kafir) according to the intent of the category, and (al-kafirun), and (al-kufr), i.e., its people, and those who disbelieved. And (sa-yu'lamu) in the passive form from the causative (i'lam), i.e., he will be informed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 13, verse 43:

(p-29) ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger."﴾ It is said: this was uttered by the chieftains of the Jews. The use of the present tense (of the verb) is to bring before the mind the image of their shameful statement, expressing astonishment at it, or to indicate that this occurs repeatedly and continuously from them.

﴿Say, "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you."﴾ For He has manifested, in support of my messengership, decisive proofs and clear evidences, such that there is no need for the testimony of any other witness. ﴿And whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ — that is, the knowledge of the Qur'an and its inimitable composition — or it means whoever is among the scholars of the People of the Book who embraced Islam, because they bear witness to his description (ﷺ) in their scriptures. The verse is Medinan by consensus. Or it means whoever has knowledge of the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), which is Allah, glory be to Him. That is: Allah is sufficient as a witness between us regarding the One who deserves worship, for He has filled His Book with the call to worship Him and has strengthened me with various kinds of support; and (He is sufficient as a witness) by virtue of His exclusive knowledge of what is in the Tablet of existing and established things, of which my messengership is part. It was also read: "min 'indihi" with a kasra (on the mim and the ha'), and "'ilmu al-Kitab" in the first reading is in the nominative, governed by the preceding adverbial phrase (as the agent of the sentence-like construction), or it is a subject whose predicate is the adverbial phrase; in the second reading it is necessarily so. It was also read: "min 'indihi 'ulima al-Kitab" with a kasra, with the passive verb form, and "al-Kitab" in the nominative.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Ra'd will be given the reward of ten good deeds, equal in weight to every cloud that has passed and every cloud that will exist until the Day of Resurrection, and he will be raised on the Day of Resurrection among those who fulfil the covenant of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

And Allah knows best what is correct.
